Suggested Book: Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces by M.Do Carmo.

Definition

1) A differentiable curve (\(C^{\infty}\)) is a \(C^{\infty}\) map \(\alpha:I\to \mathbb{R}^3,I=(a,b)\subset\mathbb{R}\). \(\alpha(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t))\),x,y,z are \(C^{\infty}\) functions.

2) The vector \(\alpha'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t),z'(t))\) is called the tangent vector of \(\alpha\) at \(\alpha(t)\).

3) \(\alpha\) is called planar if there exists a plane \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^3\) such that \(\alpha(I)\subset P\). By a rigid motion, \(\alpha(t)=(x(t),y(t),0)\).

Comment

1) \(\alpha\) is not required to be injective. e.g. \(\alpha(t)=(t^3-4t,t^2-4), t_{1,2}=\pm2, \alpha(t_1)=\alpha(t_2)=(0,0)\).

2) \(\alpha(I)\) could have corners. e.g. \(\alpha(t)=(t^2,t^3)\), \(\alpha(I)\) is the graph of \(f(x)=x^{2/3}\).

3) Even if \(\alpha\) is injective, \(\alpha\) could be not an homeomorphism onto its image. e.g.

\[ \alpha:(-1,\infty)\to \mathbb{R}^2\quad \alpha(t)=(\frac{3t}{1+t^3},\frac{3t^2}{1+t^3}) \]

Figure: Folium of Descartes

Example

1) Lines:\(\alpha(t)=tv+v_0, v,v_0\in\mathbb{R}^3, t\in\mathbb{R}\).

2) Circles: \(\alpha(t)=c+r(\cos\frac{t}{r},\sin\frac{t}{r}),c\in\mathbb{R}^2,r>0,t\in\mathbb{R}\).

3) Helices: \(\alpha(t)=(a\cos\frac{t}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}},a\sin\frac{t}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}},\frac{bt}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}),a,b\neq0,t\in\mathbb{R}\).

Length: Given \(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3,[a,b]\subset I\). What is \(L(\alpha([a,b]))\)?

Take a partition of \([a,b]\) i.e. a choice \(P=\{t_0=a<t_1<\cdots<t_n=b\}\), \(L_a^b(\alpha,P)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^n|\alpha(t_i)-\alpha(t_{i-1})|\).

\(|P|=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}|t_i-t_{i-1}|\).

Theorem

\(\forall\varepsilon>0,\exists\delta>0,s.t. |P|<\delta\implies |L_a^b(\alpha,P)-\int_a^b|\alpha'(t)|dt|<\varepsilon\).

Proposition

\(L_a^b(\alpha)=\int_a^b|\alpha'(t)|dt\).

Proof

Pf: define \(f:I\times I\times I\to \mathbb{R}\quad (t_1,t_2,t_3)\mapsto \sqrt{x'(t_1)^2+y'(t_2)^2+z'(t_3)^2}\).

\(f\) is continuous \(\implies\) uniformly continuous on \([a,b]\times[a,b]\times[a,b]=:[a,b]^3\).

So \(\forall\varepsilon>0,\exists\delta>0,s.t.\) if \((t_1,t_2,t_3)\) and \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\in[a,b]^3\) with \(|t_1-s_1|<\delta,|t_2-s_2|<\delta,|t_3-s_3|<\delta\implies |f(t_1,t_2,t_3)-f(s_1,s_2,s_3)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{b-a}\).

By the Mean Value Theorem, \(|\alpha(t_i)-\alpha(t_{i-1})|=f(\beta_i,\gamma_i,\delta_i)(t_i-t_{i-1})\), for some \(\beta_i,\gamma_i,\delta_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]\).

\(L_a^b(\alpha,P)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^mf(\beta_i,\gamma_i,\delta_i)(t_i-t_{i-1})\).

But \(\int_a^b|\alpha'(t)|dt=\sum\limits_{i=1}^m\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}|\alpha'(t)|dt=\sum\limits_{i=1}^m|\alpha'(\xi_i)|(t_i-t_{i-1})=\sum\limits_{i=1}^mf(\xi_i,\xi_i,\xi_i)(t_i-t_{i-1}),\xi_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]\).

\(|P|<\delta\implies t_i-t_{i-1}<\delta,\forall i\implies |\beta_i-\xi_i|<\delta,|\gamma_i-\xi_i|<\delta,|\delta_i-\xi_i|<\delta\).\(\square\)

Definition

\(L_a^b(\alpha)=\int_a^b|\alpha'(t)|dt\).

Check: Invariance under isometries.

Narrative

\(\alpha: I\to\mathbb{R}^3\). An isometry of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a transformation \(\varphi\) of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) s.t.$d(p,q)=d(\varphi(p),\varphi(q)),\forall p, q\implies \varphi $ is, up to a translation, a linear map whose associated matrix \(A\) satisfies \(AA^t=Id\).

Example

Lines as minimal.

\(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3,[a,b]\subset I\).

\(|\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)|\le L_a^b(\alpha)\).

\(|\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)|=|\int_a^b \alpha'(t)dt|\le\int_a^b|\alpha'(t)|dt= L_a^b(\alpha)\).

Exercise

\(|\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)|=L_a^b(\alpha)\implies\alpha\) is the segment?

Definition

A diffeomorphism \(\varphi:J\to I(I,J \text{ open intervals})\) which is \(C^{\infty}\), invertible with \(C^{\infty}\) inverse.

Given \(\alpha:I\to \mathbb{R}^3\) we can construct a new curve \(\beta:J\to\mathbb{R}^3\) as \(\beta=\alpha\circ\varphi\). \(\beta\) is called a reparametrization of \(\alpha\).

Proposition

\(\varphi:J\to I\) diffeomorphism. \(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3,[a,b]\subset\mathbb{J}\). Then \(L_a^b(\alpha\circ\varphi)=L_c^d(\alpha)\).

Proof

Pf:\(|(\alpha\circ\varphi)'(t)|=|\alpha'(\varphi(t))||\varphi'(t)|\).

\(\varphi\) diffeomorphism \(\implies\varphi'>0\) or \(\varphi'<0\) everywhere.

Call \(s=\varphi(t)\). \(\int_a^b|(\alpha\circ\varphi)'(t)|dt=\int_a^b|\alpha'(\varphi(t))||\varphi'(t)|dt=\int_c^d|\frac{d}{ds}(\alpha(s))|ds\).\(\square\)

Chapter: Curves

Narrative

We have \(\alpha:I o\mathbb{R}^3,t_0\in I\), define \(s:I o\mathbb{R}\quad t\mapsto\int_{t_0}^t|\alpha'(u)|du=L_{t_0}^t(\alpha)\). The function \(I o\mathbb{R}\quad u\mapsto|\alpha'(u)|\) is in general just continuous. \(s\) is just \(C^1\), \(s'(t)=|\alpha'(t)|\). In particular, \(s\) is not a diffeomorphism.

If \(|\alpha'(t)| eq0,\) then \(s\) is indeeed a diffeomorphism between \(I\) and \(s(I)\). Such curves are called regular.\(\implies s\in C^{\infty}\).

Call \(J=s(I),\varphi\) is the inverse of \(s\) and define \( eta(s)=\alpha\circ\varphi:J o\mathbb{R}^3\). \( eta'(s)=\alpha'(\varphi(s))\varphi'(s)= rac{\alpha'(\varphi(s))}{|\alpha'(\varphi(s))|}\). \(| eta'(s)|=1,\ orall s\in J\).

Definition

\(\alpha:I o\mathbb{R}^3\) is parametrized with arc length(p.a.l.) if \(|\alpha'(t)|=1, orall t\).

Theorem

Every regular curve can be parametrized with arc length.

Remark

\(s\) is not unique, it depends on \(t_0\) and on a constant of integration.

Example

1) Lines:\(\alpha(t)=tv+v_0,t\in\mathbb{R},t_0=0\). \(\alpha'(t)=v(v eq0), s(t)=\int_0^t|v|dt=t|v|\).

\(\varphi(s)= rac{s}{|v|}, eta(s)= rac{s}{|v|}v+v_0\).

2) \(\alpha:\mathbb{R} o\mathbb{R}^2\) Logarithmic spiral. \(t ightsquigarrow(ae^{bt}\cos t,ae^{bt}\sin t),a>0, b<0,t_0=0\).

\(s(t)=\int_0^t|(a(be^{bt}\cos t-e^{bt}\sin t),a(be^{bt}\sin t+e^{bt}\cos t))|dt=\int_0^tae^{bt}\sqrt{b^2+1}dt=( rac{e^{bt}-1}{b})a(b^2+1)^{ rac{1}{2}}\).

\(\alpha\) is p.a.l. \(T(s):=\alpha'(s)\). \(|T(s)|=1\) i.e. \(<T(s),T(s)>=1\implies <T'(s),T(s)>=0\). \(T'\) is always orthogonal to \(T\).

Definition

1) \(k(s)=|T'(s)|\) is called curvature of \(\alpha\) at \(s\).

This is only continuous. It is \(C^{\infty}\) if \(T'(s) eq0, orall s\). From now on we assume \(k(s)>0, orall s\).

2) \(N(s)= rac{T'(s)}{|T'(s)|}= rac{1}{k(s)}T'(s)\) is called the normal vector to \(\alpha\) at \(s\).

3) \(B(s):=T(s)\wedge N(s)\) is called the binormal vector to \(\alpha\) at \(s\).

4) {T(s),N(s),B(s)} is called Frenet's trihedron.

\(T'(s)=k(s)N(s)\).

$ B(s)=T(s)\wedge N(s)$.

\(B'=T'\wedge N+T\wedge N'=T\wedge N'\).

\( egin{cases} <B',T>=0\ <B',B>=0\ \end{cases}\implies B'(s)= au(s)N(s)\).

Definition

\( au(s)\) is called torsion of \(\alpha\) at \(s\).

\( au=<B',N>\).

\(T' ightsquigarrow k\).

\(B' ightsquigarrow au\).

\(N' ightsquigarrow\ ?\)

\(<N,T>=0\implies<N',T>+<N,T'>=0\).

\(<N,B>=0\implies<N',B>+<N,B'>=0\).

\(<N',T>+k(s)=0\).

\(<N',B>+ au(s)=0\).

Theorem

\(\alpha:I o\mathbb{R}^3\) p.a.l. and \(k>0\)

\[ egin{cases} T'=kN\ N'=-kT- au B\ B'= au N\ \end{cases} \] Exercise

1) Lines \(\alpha(t)=tv+v_0,|v|=1\). \(T(t)=v,T'\equiv0,k(t)\equiv0.\)

2) Circles \(\alpha(t)=r(\cos rac{t}{r},\sin rac{t}{r},0)+c\).

\(\alpha'(t)=r(-{1\over r}\sin{t\over r},{1\over r}\cos{t\over r},0)=(-\sin{t\over r},\cos{t\over r},0),|\alpha'(t)|=1, orall t\).

\(\implies t=a.l., T=\alpha'\).

\(T'=(-{1\over r}\cos{t\over r},{1\over r}\sin{t\over r},0)\implies k(t)={1 \over r}( eq0)\).

\(N=(-\cos{t\over r},\sin{t\over r},0),B(t)=(0,0,1)\implies B'=0\implies au(t)=0\).

3) Helices \(k(t)={|a| \over a^2+b^2}, au(t)=-{b \over a^2+b^2}\).

Theorem

\(\alpha:I o\mathbb{R}^3\),p.a.l., \(k>0\).\(\alpha\) is planar iff \( au\equiv0\).

Proof

Pf: Suppose \( au\equiv0:B(s)=v\) constant vector \((|v|=1)\).

\((<\alpha(s),v>)'=<T,v>=0\).

\(\implies<\alpha(s),v>=a,a\in\mathbb{R}\) which is the equation of a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).\(\square\)

Torsion measures exactly how much you have to stretch it. If a curve would like to lie on a plane, and instead you are pushing it in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) in the three space, there is some kind of effort you have to do, and this effort is measured exactly by the function \( au\).

Theorem

\(\alpha:I o\mathbb{R}^3\), p.a.l. \(k\equiv0\) iff \(\alpha\) is a piece of a line.

Proof

Pf: \(\leftharpoonup\) done.

\( ightharpoonup\) \(k\equiv0\implies \alpha'=T=v\) constant vector.

\(\alpha=tv+v_0\).\(\square\)

Chapter: Curves

\(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3\) p.a.l. \(k>0\).

\[ s\mapsto \begin{pmatrix} T(s)\\ N(s)\\ B(s)\\ \end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^9. \] \[ \begin{pmatrix} T'\\ N'\\ B'\\ \end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix} kN\\ -kT-\tau B\\ \tau N\\ \end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix} O_3 & kId_3 & O_3\\ -kId_3 & O_3 & -\tau Id_3\\ O_3 & \tau Id_3 & O_3\\ \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} T(s)\\ N(s)\\ B(s)\\ \end{pmatrix},O_3= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\ \end{pmatrix}, Id_3= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ \end{pmatrix}. \]

Theorem

Given \(k_0,\tau_0:I\to\mathbb{R},C^{\infty},k_0>0\), there exists a curve \(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3\) p.a.l. \(k(s)=k_0(s)\) and \(\tau(s)=\tau_0(s)\). Moreover, \(\alpha\) is unique up to direct isometries of \(\ \mathbb{R}^3\).

Pf: Look at \(x'(s)=A_0(s)x(s)\quad (*)\)

where \(A_0(s)=\begin{pmatrix} O_3 & k_0(s)Id_3 & O_3\\ -k_0Id_3 & O_3 & -\tau_0 Id_3\\ O_3 & \tau_0 Id_3 & O_3\\ \end{pmatrix}\).

Choose \(a\in\mathbb{R}^9\) s.t. \(t_0=(a_1,a_2,a_3),n_0=(a_4,a_5,a_6),b_0=(a_7,a_8,a_9)\) form an oriented orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

Set \(f:I\to\mathbb{R}^3\) solution of \((*)\) and define \(t=(f_1,f_2,f_3),n=(f_4,f_5,f_6),b=(f_7,f_8,f_9)\).

We want to prove that \(\{t,n,b\}\) is an O.N.（注：orthonormal）\((>0)\) basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\ \forall s\in I\): look at \(M(s)=\begin{pmatrix} <t,t> & <t,n> & <t,b>\\ <t,n> & <n,n> & <n,b>\\ <t,b> & <n,b> & <b,b>\\ \end{pmatrix}\).

\((*)\implies 2M'(s)=A(s)M(s)-M(s)A(s)\) where \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & k_0 & 0\\ -k_0 & 0 & -\tau_0\\ 0 & \tau_0 & 0\\ \end{pmatrix},M(0)=Id_3\). But \(M(s)=Id_3,\forall s\) is a solution.

\(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3\quad s\mapsto\int_{s_0}^st(u)du\).\(\square\)

Simple（注：simple means no self-intersection） closed（注：closed means \(\alpha(a)=\alpha(b)\)） planar curves: \(\alpha:I=[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^2\).

Circa 250 B.C. Isoperimetric problem:

Among all planar simple closed curves of length \(L\), which one bounds the region of largest area?

Circa 200 AD, Pappus.

Virgilius, Dido, circa 50 AD.

Weierstrass, circa 1870. Schimidt, circa 1940.（注：for more information about the history of Isoperimetric problem, you can refer to the book The Parsimonious Universe, Anthony Tromba）

Green's theorem: \(f(x,y),g(x,y)\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^2)\). \(R\) is the bounded region inside a curve \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^2\), then \(\int_R({\partial g\over \partial x}-{\partial f\over \partial y})dxdy=\int_C(f{dx\over dt}+g{dy\over dt})dt\).

Take \(f=-y,g=x,2 Area(R)=\int_a^b(x(t){dy\over dt}-y(t){dx\over dt})dt\).

Theorem: \(L^2\ge4\pi Area(R).\) Moreover \(L^2=4\pi Area(R)\) iff \(\alpha\) parametrizes a circle.

If \(C\) is parametrized by a.l. as \(\alpha(s)=(x(s),y(s))\), we can choose a parametrization of \(C^1\) as \(\beta(s)=(x(s),\overline{y}(s)),s\in[0,L]\).

\(Area(R)=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^L(xy'-x'y)(s)ds=\int_0^Lxy'ds\).

\(Area(\text{interior of }C')=\pi r^2=-\int_0^Lx\overline{y}ds\).

\(Area(R)+\pi r^2=\int_0^L(xy'-\overline{y}x')ds\le\int_0^L\sqrt{(xy'-\overline{y}x')^2}ds\le\int_0^L\sqrt{(x^2+\overline{y}^2)((x')^2+(y')^2)}ds=\int_0^L\sqrt{(x^2+\overline{y}^2)}ds=Lr.\)

\(\sqrt{Area(R)}\sqrt{\pi r^2}\le\frac{1}{2}(Area(R)+\pi r^2)\le\frac{Lr}{2}\).

"=" as an exercise.

docs.text:
Chapter: Regular Surfaces

Circa 1800. 1827 Disquisiciones Superficies Curvas, Gauss.

Definition

A subset \(S\) of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a regular surface if \( orall p\in S,\exists\) open set \(V\subset\mathbb{R}^3\) s.t. \(p\in V\) and \(\exists X:U o V\cap S\), where \(U\) open set of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \(X\) surjective and:

1) \(X\) is \(C^{\infty}, (u,v)\in U, X(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v))\) i.e. \(x,y,z\) are \(C^{\infty}\) on \(U\).

2) \(X\) is a homeomorphism.

3) \( orall q\in U,dX_q:\mathbb{R}^2 o\mathbb{R}^3\) is injective.

\(X\) is called local parametrization or local chart around \(p\). \(V\cap S\) is called coordinate chart of \(S\) at \(p\).

Rem（注：reminder）: \(dX_q:\mathbb{R}^2 o\mathbb{R}^3\), given \(w\in\mathbb{R}^2,\exists\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) o U\) s.t. \(\alpha(0)=q,\alpha'(0)=w\).

Set \( eta=X\circ\alpha,dX_q(w)= eta'(0).\)

\(\{e_1,e_2\}\) standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2,e_1=(1,0),e_2=(0,1)\).

\(\{f_1,f_2,f_3\}\) standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

\(\alpha(t)=(u(t),v(t)),\alpha'(0)=u'(0)e_1+v'(0)e_2\).

Narrative

\( eta(t)=(x(u(t),v(t)),y(u(t),v(t)),z(u(t),v(t))), eta'(t)=( rac{\partial x}{\partial u} rac{du}{dt}+ rac{\partial x}{\partial v} rac{dv}{dt})f_1+( rac{\partial y}{\partial u} rac{du}{dt}+ rac{\partial y}{\partial v} rac{dv}{dt})f_2+( rac{\partial z}{\partial u} rac{du}{dt}+ rac{\partial z}{\partial v} rac{dv}{dt})f_3= egin{pmatrix} rac{\partial x}{\partial u} & rac{\partial x}{\partial v}\ rac{\partial y}{\partial u} & rac{\partial y}{\partial v}\ rac{\partial z}{\partial u} & rac{\partial z}{\partial v}\ \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} rac{du}{dt}\ rac{dv}{dt}\ \end{pmatrix}\) at \(t=0\).

\(dX_q\) injective \(\iff\) \( rac{\partial x}{\partial u}, rac{\partial x}{\partial v}\) linearly independent \( orall q( rac{\partial x}{\partial u}\wedge rac{\partial x}{\partial v} eq0)\).

Regular surfaces do not have self-intersection.

Proposition

\(f:U o\mathbb{R},C^{\infty},\Gamma_f=\{(u,v,f(u,v))\mid (u,v)\in U\}\) is a regular surface.

Proof

Pf: \(X(u,v)=(u,v,f(u,v))\)

\(X\) is \(C^{\infty}\).

\(X\) is 1:1.

\(X^{-1}\) is \(C^{\infty}\) because it is the restriction to \(\Gamma_f\) of \((x,y,z) o(x,y)\).

\(dX_q\) injective \(\iff rac{\partial x}{\partial u}, rac{\partial x}{\partial v}\) linearly independent.

\( rac{\partial x}{\partial u}=(1,0, rac{\partial f}{\partial u}), rac{\partial x}{\partial v}=(0,1, rac{\partial f}{\partial v})\).\(\square\)

Exercise

\(S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}\).（注：\(S^2\) will mean always the sphere of radius 1 and center the origin）

\(X_1(x,y)=(x,y,\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}),(x,y)\in U,U=\{(x,y)\mid x^2+y^2<1\},X_2(x,y)=(x,y,-\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2})\).

\(X_3(x,z)=(x,\sqrt{1-x^2-z^2},z),U'=\{(x,z)\mid x^2+z^2<1\},X_4(x,z)=(x,-\sqrt{1-x^2-z^2},z)\).

\(X_{5,6}=(\pm\sqrt{1-y^2-z^2},y,z)\).

We have proved that the sphere is a regular surface by covering it with six charts.

So, in principle, you would ask, as a mathematician, which is the least possible number of charts? It is possible to cover a sphere with one chart?

Narrative

The definition of a regular surface requires \(X\) to be an homeomorphism between the domain and the target. So if your surface is covered by one chart in particular, that means that your surface is homeomorphic to a domain of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). By definition, the sphere is compact, an open domain of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) will never be compact. So the answer is no, and in fact, we can cover a sphere with two charts.

Implicit Function Theorem:

Narrative

Let \(\mathcal{O}\) be an open set of \(\mathbb{R}^3,p=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\in\mathcal{O},a\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(f:\mathcal{O} o\mathbb{R},c^{\infty}\). Suppose \(f(p)=a, rac{\partial f}{\partial z}(p) eq0\). Then \(\exists\) open set \(U\) s.t. \((x_0,y_0)\in U\) and an open set \(V\subset\mathbb{R}\) with \(z_0\in V\) and a \(C^{\infty}\) function \(g:U o V\) s.t. \(U imes V\subset\mathcal{O}\), \(g(x_0,y_0)=z_0\) and \(\{q\in U imes V\mid f(q)=a\}=\{(x,y,g(x,y))\mid (x,y)\in U\}\).

Corollary

Let \(a\in\mathbb{R}\) be a regular value of a \(C^{\infty}\) function \(f\), i.e. \(df_p eq0, orall p\in f^{-1}(a)\). \(f^{-1}(a)\) is either empty or a regular surface.

Proof

Pf: Let \(p=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\in f^{-1}(a),df_p eq0.\) Assume \( rac{\partial f}{\partial z}(p) eq0\). IFT（注：Implicit function theorem） \((S=f^{-1}(a)) S\cap(U imes V)\) is the graph of a \(C^{\infty}-\)function.\(\square\)

Example

Quadrics

Let \(A\) be a \(4 imes4\) symmetric matrix. Let \(S=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid (1\ v^t)A egin{pmatrix}1\ v\\end{pmatrix}=0\}\).

Look at \(f(v)=(1\ v^t)A egin{pmatrix}1\ v\\end{pmatrix},f:\mathbb{R}^3 o\mathbb{R},S=f^{-1}(0)\).

Is 0 a regular value for \(f\)?

Pick \(v\in f^{-1}(o)\) and compute \(df_v\).

\(df_v(w)= rac{d}{dt}(f\circ\alpha)(0)\), take \(\alpha(t)\) s.t. \(\alpha(0)=v,\alpha'(0)=w\).

\(f\circ\alpha(t)=(1\ v^t)A egin{pmatrix}1\ v\\end{pmatrix}\).

\( rac{d}{dt} igg|_{t=0}=(0\ w^t)A egin{pmatrix}1\ v\\end{pmatrix}+(1\ v^t)A egin{pmatrix}0\ w\\end{pmatrix}=2(1\ v^t)A egin{pmatrix}0\ w\\end{pmatrix}\).

\(df_v(w)=0, orall w\iff (1\ v^t)A=(\lambda,0)\). \(v\in f^{-1}(0)\implies\lambda=0\).

0 is not regular value iff \((1\ v^t)A=0\) has solution.

docs.text:
Chapter: Regular Surfaces

Example

\(S^1(r)\) circle of radius \(r(r>0)\) in the plane \(x=0\) with center \((0,a,0),(a>r)\).

Rotate this curve around the axis \(z\),\(\{x=y=0\}.\) \(S=\{(x,y,z)\mid (\sqrt{z^2+y^2}-a)^2+x^2=r^2\}\).

Look at \(f:\mathbb{R}^3\backslash\{z-\text{axis}\}（注：I've taken out the z-axis in order to have a differentiable function. Otherwise, since I have a square root here, I would end up in problems of differentiability.）\to\mathbb{R}\quad (x,y,z)\mapsto (\sqrt{z^2+y^2}-a)^2+x^2\).

\(S=f^{-1}(r^2)\).

Is \(r^2\) a regular value for \(f\)? \(df_p,\forall p\in f^{-1}(r^2)\).

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2x,\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{2y(\sqrt{z^2+y^2}-a)}{\sqrt{z^2+y^2}},\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=\frac{2z(\sqrt{z^2+y^2}-a)}{\sqrt{z^2+y^2}}\).

\(r^2\) is a regular value.

Definition

\(S\) is a regular surface, \(\mathcal{O}\) is an open set of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

A) \(F:S\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable if for any local chart of \(S, X:U\to S, F\circ X:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable.

B) \(f:\mathcal{O}\to S\) is differentiable if \(f:\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}^3\) is differentiable.

C) \(S_1\) ia another regular surface, \(f:S\to S_1\) is differentiable if \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}^3\) is differentiable（注：in the sense of A)）.

\(f,g:S\to\mathbb{R}^n\) are differentiable, then \(f+g,\lambda f,<f,g>\) are differentiable.

Example

1) \(F:\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}^3\) is differentiable and \(S\subset\mathcal{O}\). \(F\bigg|_{S}\) is differentiable. In particular, \(i:S\to\mathbb{R}^3\) and \(id:S\to S\) and the constants are differentiable.

2) height function: let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^3\) be a plane, \(p_0\in P\) and \(a\) is a normal vector to \(P\). \(S\) is a regular surface, \(h:S\to \mathbb{R}\quad p\mapsto<p-p_0,a>\) is differentiable.

3) distance squared: \(p_0\in\mathbb{R}^3\).

\(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\quad p\mapsto|p-p_0|^2\).

4) distance: \(f(p)=|p-p_0|\quad\) \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\).

If \(p_0\notin S\), then differentiable.

If \(p_0\in S\), then not differentiable.

Proposition

\(f:S\to\mathbb{R}^n\) function. If \(\forall p\in S,\exists x_p:U_p\to S\) local chart around \(p\) s.t. \(f\circ x_p:U_p\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is differentiable, then \(f\) is differentiable.

Pf: Exercise.

Definition

\(S\) is a regular surface. \(p\in S\). We say that \(v\in\mathbb{R}^3\) is a tangent vector to \(S\) at \(p\) if \(\exists\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to S\) differentiable, \(\varepsilon>0\), s.t. \(\alpha(0)=p,\alpha'(0)=v\).

The set of tangent vectors to \(S\) at \(p\) is denoted by \(T_pS\).

Lemma

\(X:U\to S\) is a local chart around \(p\). \(T_pS=dX_{X^{-1}(p)}(\mathbb{R}^2)\).

Proof

Pf: \("\supseteq"\) Let \(w\in\mathbb{R}^2\) be any vector.

\(\beta(t)=X^{-1}(p)+tw,\beta:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to U\).

\(\beta(0)=X^{-1}(p),\beta'(0)=w\).

Define \(\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to S,\alpha=X\circ \beta\).

\(\alpha(0)=p,\alpha'(0)=dX_{X^{-1}(p)}(w)\).

\(\implies dX_{X^{-1}(p)}(w)\in T_pS\).

\("\subseteq"\) Let \(v\in T_pS\). \(\exists\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to S,\alpha(0)=p,\alpha'(0)=v\).

\(\alpha(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\subset X(U)\).

Put \(\beta=X^{-1}\circ\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to U\).

\(\beta(0)=X^{-1}(p)\).

\(v=\alpha'(0)=(X\circ \beta)'(0)=dX_{X^{-1}(p)}(\beta'(0))\).\(\square\)

The tangent space to a regular surface at any point is automatically a two-dimensional vector space.

Corollary

1) \(T_pS\) is a vector space.

2) \(T_pS\) is generated by \(\{\frac{\partial X}{\partial u},\frac{\partial X}{\partial v}\}\).

Figure: The warning of drawing tangent space

Narrative

General warning, when you draw pictures, so you draw your surface, and both me and books and whatever, you will always find a picture of this form. So this is the surfaces, this is the point \(p\) (fig:The warning of drawing tangent space), and everybody will draw something like this as the tangent space. You image this two-dimensional vector space translated with origin at the point \(p\). The truth is not this one. This is just to fix in your mind that this is the tangent space at the point \(p\). If you really want to draw which space it is, which set it is, since it's vector space, it's better passed through the origin. So it's really the translation of what you draw in this geometric way here. We will always make this mistake happily.

Exercise

1) \(\mathcal{O}\) open set of \(\mathbb{R}^3, f:\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}\) is a differentiable function. \(a\) is a regular value of \(f\). \(S=f^{-1}(a)\) is a regular surface.

Claim: \(T_pS=ker((df_p):\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R})\).

Pf: \("\subseteq"\) \(v\in T_pS\implies \exists\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to S\) s.t. \(\alpha(0)=p,\alpha'(0)=v\implies f(\alpha(t))=a,\forall t\implies df_p(v)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}(f(\alpha(t)))=0\).

We know by general theory that \(ker((df_p):\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R})\) is two-dimensional, and we just proved that \(T_pS\) is contained in \(ker((df_p):\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R})\). But \(T_pS\) is also two-dimensional by general theory. So this is a two-dimensional vector space contained in a two-dimensional vector space. So there is nothing to prove. They have to be the same.\(\square\)

2) \(S_a^2(r)=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid |p-a|^2=r^2\}\).

\(f(p)=|p-a|^2,S_a^2(r)=f^{-1}(r^2)\).

\(df_p(v)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}<\alpha(t)-a,\alpha(t)-a>=<v,p-a>+<p-a,v>=2<v,p-a>\).

\(T_pS_a^2(r)=ker\ df_p=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid<v,p-a>=0\}\).

Chapter: Regular Surfaces

Definition

\(f:S\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is a differentiable map. \(p\in S,v\in T_pS\) \((\exists\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to S,\alpha(0)=p,\alpha'(0)=v)\). \(df_p(v)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}(f\circ \alpha)(t)=(f\circ\alpha)'(0)\).

Proposition

\(df_p(v)\) is well-defined.

Proof

Pf: Let \(X:U\to S\) be a local chart around \(p\).

\(T_pS=dX_{X^{-1}(p)}(\mathbb{R}^2),q=X^{-1}(p)\).

\(\alpha(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\subset X(U)\).

The curve \(X^{-1}\circ\alpha:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to U\).

\((X^{-1}\circ\alpha)(0)=q,\alpha=X\circ(X^{-1}\circ\alpha)\).

Taking derivative at \(t=0\), we get \(dX_{q}((X^{-1}\circ\alpha)'(0))=v\implies (X^{-1}\circ\alpha)'(0)=(dX_q)^{-1}(v)\).

But \((f\circ\alpha)'(0)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}(f\circ X)\circ(X^{-1}\circ\alpha)=d(f\circ X)_q((X^{-1}\circ\alpha)'(0))=d(f\circ X)_q[(dX_q)^{-1}(v)]\implies df_p(v)=d(f\circ X)_q[(dX_q)^{-1}(v)]\).

\(df_p=d(f\circ X)_q[(dX_q)^{-1}]\) does not depend on \(\alpha\).

The only problem coming from the definition is \(\alpha\), is not \(X\).

So if I give you a formula for the differential which does not contain \(\alpha\), I'm done.\(\square\)

If \(f:S\to S_1,\forall p\in S,\forall v\in T_pS, df_p(v)\in T_{f(p)}S_1\).

All the algebraic properties that held for Euclidean spaces holds also now.

\(S_1\xrightarrow{f}S_2\xrightarrow{g}S_3\quad\) \(d(g\circ f)_p=dg_{f(p)}\circ df_p\).

We will refer to this as kind of the chain rule for maps between surfaces.

Example

1) \(A\) is a symmetric（注：symmetric means \(<Av,w>=<v,Aw>,\forall v,w\in\mathbb{R}^3\)） \(3\times 3\) matrix.

One of the basic properties that you know about symmetric matrices: they are diagonalizable with an orthonormal basis.

Let's see if we can prove it, at least in dimension three, using the notion of the differentiable of a map.

Let \(f:S_0^2(1)\to\mathbb{R}\quad p\mapsto<Ap,p>\).

\(v\in T_pS_0^2(1),df_p(v)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}(f\circ\alpha)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}<A\alpha(t),\alpha(t)>=<A\alpha'(0),\alpha(0)>+<A\alpha(0),\alpha'(0)>=<Av,p>+<Ap,v>=2<Ap,v>\).

\(p\) is a critical point（注：critical point: \(p\in S_0^2(1)\) s.t. \(df_p\equiv0\)） iff \(Ap=\lambda p\) for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). Since \(\langle Ap,p\rangle=\lambda\), this is equivalent to \(Ap=f(p)p\).

Claim: there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors for \(A\).

1) If \(f\) is constant \(\implies A=\mu Id\quad\) Done.

2) If \(f\) is not constant, \(S_0^2(1)\) is compact. \(\exists p_1,p_2\in S_0^2(1)\) maximal and minimal for \(f\).

\(p_1,p_2\) are eigenvectors of norm 1.

Claim: \(p_1\perp p_2\): \((f(p_1)-f(p_2))<p_1,p_2>=<f(p_1)p_1,p_2>-<p_1,f(p_2)p_2>=<Ap_1,p_2>-<p_1,Ap_2>=0\implies <p_1,p_2>=0\).

I know that this matrix \(A\) has two orthogonal matrices, eigenvectors of norm one. I missed one, there should be a third one. But actually you see, up to now, \(\mathbb{R}^3\) was irrelevant. You could have taken a symmetric \(n\times n\) object, and these two would be there. Now, that's the only moment where the final part of the proof works only because you are in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). If you have two eigenvectors orthogonal, where is the only possible third one? So you just take the wedge of those two and you check that it works. It's the only possibility. There is nothing else.

2) \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^3,p_0\in\mathbb{R}^3\).

\(f(p)=|p-p_0|^2,f:S\to\mathbb{R}\).

I would like to understand what are the critical points of this map.

\(v\in T_pS:df_p(v)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}(f\circ \alpha)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}<\alpha(t)-p_0,\alpha(t)-p_0>=2<v,p-p_0>\).

\(p\) is a critical point for \(f\) iff the normal line to \(S\) at \(p\) passes through \(p_0\).

If \(S\) is compact, there are at least 2 critical points. The normal line that the critical points must hit is \(p_0\), so every point of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) lies on the normal line, at least one, maybe more.

If \(\exists p_0\) s.t. each normal line to \(S\) passes through \(p_0\). then \(S\cong"S_{p_0}^2(r)"\) open subset. i.e. if all the normals to a connected surface pass through the same point, then the surface is an open set of the sphere.

Chapter: The Geometry of the Gauss Map

Definition

\(S\) is a regular surface. A vector field \(V\) on \(S\) is a differentiable function \(V:S o\mathbb{R}^3\). \(V\) is called normal (unitary) if \( orall p\in S,V(p)\perp T_pS\ (|V(p)|=1)\).

Example

\(S=\{2z=x^2+y^2\}\).

\(S=\Gamma_f,f:\mathbb{R}^2 o\mathbb{R}\quad (x,y)\mapsto rac{1}{2}(x^2+y^2)\).

\(X:\mathbb{R}^2 o\mathbb{R}^3\quad (u,v)\mapsto(u,v, rac{1}{2}(u^2+v^2))\).

\(\{ rac{\partial X}{\partial u}, rac{\partial X}{\partial v}\},X_u=(1,0,u),X_v=(0,1,v)\).

\(p=X_(u_0,v_0),T_pS=span\{X_u(u_0,v_0),X_v(u_0,v_0)\}\).

Now, the problem is, how many normal vectors do we have at a given point? Two.

Narrative

Now, the point is, the normal vectors were at a fixed point. Now let's start moving the point and let's see what happens. I mean, how many choices we have globally on a surface of unitary normal vectors. So let's see first what happens not globally on the surface, but on the piece of the surface which is covered by a chart.

Lemma

\(X;U o S\) is a local chart. Then there exists at least one unitary normal vector field on \(X(U)\).

Proof

Pf:notation:\( rac{\partial X}{\partial u}=X_u, rac{\partial X}{\partial v}=X_v\).

\(\{X_u,X_v\}\) is a basis of \(T_{X(q)}S,q\in U\).

Put \(N^X(q)= rac{X_u(q)\wedge X_v(q)}{|X_u(q)\wedge X_v(q)|}\).

\(N^X:U o\mathbb{R}^3\) is differentiable. \(N^X(q)\perp T_{X(q)}S,|N^X(q)|=1\).

Define \(N(p)=N^X\circ X^{-1}(p)\).\(\square\)

Lemma

\(S\) is connected. \(N_1,N_2\) are unitary normal vector fields on \(S\). Then either \(N_1=N_2\) or \(N_1=-N_2\).

Proof

Pf:\( orall p\in S, N_1(p),N_2(p)\) are unitary normals at \(p\), so \(N_1(p)=N_2(p)\) or \(N_1(p)=-N_2(p)\).

\(S=A\cup B,A=\{p\in S\mid N_1(p)=N_2(p)\},B=\{q\in S\mid N_1(q)=-N_2(q)\}\).

\(A,B\) closed \(\implies\) \(A\) or \(B\) empty.\(\square\)

So on a whole connected component, I have only two choices of unitary normal. But now the question is, does there always exist a unitary normal on a surface? Remember, locally, yes, because every surface is \(X\) of \(U\). So on the piece of the surface which is given like \(X\) of \(U\) for some chart, there is a unitary normal. But who is going to tell me if there is a unitary normal over the whole surface? In fact, it may be false. So the surface where a unitary normal exists are special.

Definition

A regular surface \(S\), s.t., \(\exists\) unitary normal \(N:S o\mathbb{R}^3\), is called orientable.

Example

1) \(S_{p_0}^2(r)\).

\(N:S_{p_0}^2(r) o\mathbb{R}^3\quad p\mapsto rac{1}{r}(p-p_0)\).

2) \(S=\Gamma_f\quad X(u,v)=(u,v,f(u,v))\).

\(N^X= rac{(1,0,f_u)\wedge (0,1,f_v)}{|(1,0,f_u)\wedge (0,1,f_v)|}= rac{(f_u,f_v,-1)}{\sqrt{1+f_u^2+f_v^2}}\).

3) \(S=f^{-1}(a),p \in S\). \(T_pS=ker\ df_p=\{v\in \mathbb{R}^3\mid< abla f(p),v>=0\}\).

\(N= rac{ abla f}{| abla f|}\).

The key problem of this course is, what does it mean that something is flat? And what does it mean that something has some curvature.

\(N:S o\mathbb{R}^3\) unitary normal, \(|N(p)|=1\).

\(N:S o S_0^2(1)\) is called Gauss map.

\(dN_p:T_pS o T_{N(p)}S_0^2(1)\simeq\{N(p)\}^{\perp}\simeq T_pS\).

\(dN_p:T_pS o T_pS\).

Theorem

\(dN_p\) is a symmetric（注：symmetric means \(<dN_p(v),w>=<v,dN_p(w)>, orall v,w\in T_pS\)） endomorphism（注：endomorphism means just it's a nomomorphism of vectors of the vector space to itself） of \(T_pS\).

Proof

Pf: It is enough to check it on basis. \(p\in S,X:U o S\) chart around \(p\). \(\{X_u,X_v\}\) basis of \(T_pS\).

\(\alpha(t)=X(u(t),v(t)),\alpha(0)=p\).

\(dN_p(\alpha'(0))=dN_p(u'(0)X_u+v'(0)X_v)=u'(0)dN_p(X_u)+v'(0)dN_p(X_v)=u'(0)N_u+v'(0)N_v\).

\( rac{\partial}{\partial v}<N,X_u>=0=<N_v,X_u>+<N,X_{uv}>\).

\( rac{\partial}{\partial u}<N,X_v>=0=<N_u,X_v>+<N,X_{vu}>\).

\(<N_u,X_v>=<X_u,N_v>=-<N,X_{uv}>\).\(\square\)

Definition

1) \(\mathrm{II}_p:T_pS imes T_pS o\mathbb{R}\quad (v,w)\mapsto -<dN_p(v),w>\) is called the second fundamental form of \(S\) at \(p\).

2) \(\mathrm{I}_p: T_pS imes T_pS o\mathbb{R}\quad (v,w)\mapsto <v,w>\) is called the first fundamental form \(S\) at \(p\).

3) \(N_p\) symmetric \(\implies\) diagonalizable.

\(k_1(p),k_2(p)\) the eigenvalues of \(-dN_p\ (k_1(p)\le k_2(p))\) are called principal curvature of \(S\) at \(p\).

4) \(K(p)=k_1(p)\cdot k_2(p)\) is called Gauss(ian) curvature of \(S\) at \(p\).

5) \(H(p)= rac{1}{2}(k_1(p)+k_2(p))\) is called the Mean curvature of \(S\) at \(p\).

6) the directions associated to the eigenvectors

\(v_1,v_2\) associated to \(k_1,k_2\) are called principal directions.

7) \(\alpha:I o S\) is called a line of curvature if \(\alpha'(t)\) is a principal direction of \(S\) at \(\alpha(t), orall t\).

Example

0) \(S=\)plane \(N:S o S^2\).

\(dN_p(v)=0, orall v\).

principal curvature of the plane, both zero.

Gauss curvature: zero.

Mean curvature: zero.

principal directions: There are infinitely many in this case, every direction is a principal direction.

lines of curvature: any curve on a plane.

1) \(S=S_{p_0}^2(r)\).

\(N:S_{p_0}^2(r) o S^2\quad p\mapsto rac{1}{r}(p-p_0)\).

\(dN_p(v)= rac{1}{r}v\).

\(\mathrm{II}_p(v,w)=- rac{1}{r}<v,w>\).

\(H(p)=k_1(p)=k_2(p)=- rac{1}{r}, orall p\).

\(K(p)= rac{1}{r^2}\).

Any tangent direction is a principal direction.

Any curve is a line of curvature.

Choice of the orientation has the effect of switching sign to \(H,k_1\) and \(k_2\) and it's irrelevant for the Gauss curvature.

docs.text:
Chapter: The Geometry of the Gauss Map

Example

3) Cylinder: \(S=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid x^2+y^2=r^2\},r>0\).

\(f(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2,S=f^{-1}(r^2)\).

\(df_p=2(x,y,0), abla f_p=2(x,y,0),N(p)= rac{ abla f_p}{| abla f_p|}= rac{1}{r}(x,y,0).\)

\(T_pS=ker\ df_p=\{v\mid < abla f_p,v>=0\},v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)\).

\(dN_p(v)= rac{d}{dt} igg|_{t=0}(N\circ\alpha)(t)= rac{d}{dt} igg|_{t=0} rac{1}{r}(x(t),y(t),0)= rac{1}{r}(v_1,v_2,0)\).

\(\mathrm{II}_p(v,w)=- rac{1}{r}(v_1w_1+v_2w_2)\).

\(v\) vertical（注：vertical means it has only z component）, \(dN_p(v)=0\).

\(v\) tangent to the circle, \(dN_p(v)= rac{1}{r}v\).

\(k_1(p)=- rac{1}{r},k_2(p)=0\).

\(K(p)=0,H(p)=- rac{1}{2r}\).

If it's a plane, \(K\) is zero, but it's not the unique surface having zero curvature. What's going on? I don't want to give you the answer now, but focus on this problem.

Geometric Meaning of \(\mathrm{II}_p\):

Definition

\(\alpha:I o S\) regular curve, \(\alpha(0)=p\).

\(k\) curvature of \(\alpha\) as a curve in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).（注：If I study the surface, I have a normal vector to the curve, and we called it capital \(N\), unfortunately. So now we have to distinguish the two. Because there is absolutely no reason why the normal to the surface and the normal to the curve should have anything to do at all.）

\(\cos heta=<n,N>\), \(n\) normal to \(\alpha\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

\(k_n=k\cos heta\) is called the normal curvature of \(\alpha\) at \(p\).

Of course, \(k_n\) depends not just on \(\alpha\), but on \(S\). So in some sense, it's the projection of the curvature to the surface.

Now suppose that \(\alpha\) is p.a.l. \(N(s)=N(\alpha(s))\).

\(<N(s),\alpha'(s)>\equiv0\implies <N',\alpha'>+<N,\alpha''>=0\).

\(\mathrm{II}_p(\alpha'(0),\alpha'(0))=-<dN_p(\alpha'(0)),\alpha'(0)>=-<N'(0),\alpha'(0)>=<N(p),\alpha''(0)>=<N(p),k(p)n(p)>=k_n(p)\).

So if \(v\in T_pS,|v|=1,\mathrm{II}_p(v)\) is equal to the normal curvature of any curve passing through \(p\) with velocity \(v\).

Theorem

Any curve passing through the point with a given velocity has the same normal curvature.

The eigenvalues of the quadratic form are the critical points of the value of the quadratic form restricted to the sphere in the vector space.

\(k_1(p),k_2(p)\) are the minimum and maximum of \(\mathrm{II}_p\) restricted to the vectors of \(|\cdot|=1\).

If I take any curve passing through the point on the surface, its normal curvature is bounded between \(k_1\) and \(k_2\).

\(e_1,e_2\) O.N. basis of \(T_pS\) of eigenvectors of \(-dN_p\), \(v=\cos heta\ e_1+\sin heta\ e_2\).

Narrative

(Euler's Formula) \(k_n(v)=\mathrm{II}_p(v)=-<dN_p(v),v>=-<dN_p(\cos heta\ e_1+\sin heta\ e_2),\cos heta\ e_1+\sin heta\ e_2>=-<\cos heta\ k_1e_1+\sin heta\ k_2e_2,\cos heta\ e_1+\sin heta\ e_2>=-\cos^2 heta\ k_1-\sin^2 heta\ k_2\).

Definition

\(p\in S\) is called

1) elliptic if \(K(p)>0\).

2) hyperbolic if \(K(p)<0\).

3) parabolic if \(K(p)=0,dN_p eq0\).（注：But we have two ways of getting zero curvature. And here we want to make a difference the plane and the cylinder. The Gauss curvature is the product of th two numbers. It can be zero in two ways. They are both zero or one is zero and the other is not. See, and this is exactly the difference between plane and cylinder. Parabolic is somehow the cylinder in your mind.）

4) planar if \(K(p)=0,dN_p\equiv0\).

5) if \(k_1(p)=k_2(p)\), \(p\) is called umbilical.

Do planar points characterize the plane? I mean, the number is no. There are surfaces which have planar points, and the surfaces are not the plane.

Exercise

\(S_{p_0}^2(r)\) is made of umbilical points.

Note that if a surface has an umbilical point, then it is a plane or a sphere. That would be really too much. One point cannot tell you the global geometry of a surface.

Proposition

If \(S\) is connected（注：because otherwise you have to argue on each connected component. In principle, your surface would be a plane and a sphere. As long as they don't touch, a plane union a sphere, it's a regular surface） and every \(p\in S\) is umbilical, then \(S\) is contained in a plane or in a sphere.（注：I cannot say \(S\) is a plane or a sphere because maybe it's just a piece of.）

Proof

Pf: \(X:U o S\) local chart. \(w\in T_pS,w=aX_u+bX_v,dN_p(w)=\lambda(p)w\).

In fact, I want now, in some sense, to prove that \(\lambda\) does not depend on \(p\). That's the line of the proof.

\(aN_u+bN_v=\lambda(p)(aX_u+bX_v), orall a,b\).

\(\implies\)（注：\(\lambda\) in principle was nothing. Had no regularity whatever. You can argue automatically that it should be a continuous function. Because it's the eigenvalue of a differentiable family of maps. But eigenvalues of a differentiable family of maps are just continuous. They're not more than continuous.） $N_u=\lambda X_u,N_u=\lambda X_v\implies \lambda $ is \(C^{\infty}\).

\(\lambda_vX_u+\lambda X_{uv}=\lambda_uX_v+\lambda X_{uv}\).

\(\lambda_vX_u=\lambda_uX_v\implies \lambda_u=\lambda_v=0\).

1) If \(\lambda=0\implies N\) is constant \(\implies\subset\) plane.

2) \(\lambda eq0\implies X(u,v)- rac{1}{\lambda}N(u,v)=c\) constant vector \(\implies |X(u,v)-c|^2= rac{1}{|\lambda|^2}\).

Just one thing, how come in our computation, \(\lambda\), which is the \(k_1\) or \(k_2\)? In our computation, it was plus or minus one over \(r\). Why you should not be surprised? So you could have said, well, if this \(\lambda\) is negative, it's a sphere. But no, this is dearly a wrong theorem. Because if I switch \(N\), you see, in this proposition, there is no \(N\). So \(\lambda\) on the same surface can be positive or negative because I pick one choice of \(N\), I get positive, for example, I mean, in the way we compute it, we got negative. If we do the other choice, we got positive. So you see, there is no case two \(\lambda\) positive, case three \(\lambda\) negative. It would be completely wrong. So zero and no zero, these are the only two geometric distinctions. But positive or negative here, it would be crazy.

What do we prove up to now? We have proved that the image of a chart is contained either in a plane or in the sphere. But then the whole, since every point is contained in a chart. So there is only one thing to be worried about. Would it be possible, on a surface, to have two charts: one contains on a sphere of some center and some radius and the other one contained either in another sphere of another center and another radius, or, even worse, on a plane. So I mean, why these two cases? These two cases were built with the local chart, so if you change chart, in principle, you could jump from one to two. And in fact, two, you could jump from different centers and different radius. But no, by continuity. This function \(\lambda\), is defined over the whole surface and it's continuous over the whole surface. So I mean, \(\lambda\) cannot be one here and zero here. In principle it could, but since I could join on the surface, I can go from any one point to the other with a sequence of charts intersecting each other. Of course, by connectness. But then, on the overlap, \(\lambda\) has to be constant. So it has to be the same on the two sides. So certainly I cannot pass from a sphere to a sphere, the two spheres must have the same radius. So now is it possible from one sphere to the other sphere of the same radius, I change center? Exercise. But this in principle, is possible from the way we have built things, because \(c\), which is the center of the sphere, is just kind of a constant of integration.\(\square\)

Proposition

\(K\) and \(H\) are smooth functions. \(k_1,k_2\) are continuous functions, smooth on the open set of non-umbilical points.

Proof

Pf: \(X:U o S\) local chart, \(N= rac{X_u\wedge X_v}{|X_u\wedge X_v|},X_u,X_v.\)

\(\mathrm{I}_p o M\)（注：the first fundamental form is represented by the matrix \(M\)） \(\qquad\mathrm{II}_p o \sum\qquad\) \(-dN_p o A\).

\(M= egin{pmatrix} |X_u|^2 & <X_u,X_v>\ <X_u,x_v> & |X_v|^2\ \end{pmatrix},E=|X_u|^2,F=<X_u,X_v>,G=|X_v|^2\).

\(\sum= egin{pmatrix} e & f\ f & g\ \end{pmatrix},e=\mathrm{II}_p(X_u,X_u)=<N,X_{uu}>=-<N_u,X_u>,f=\mathrm{II}_p(X_u,X_v)=<N,X_{uv}>,e=\mathrm{II}_p(X_v,X_v)=<N,X_{vv}>.\)

\((a_{ij})=A=-(+?)M^{-1}\sum=- egin{pmatrix} E & F\ F & G\ \end{pmatrix}^{-1} egin{pmatrix} e & f\ f & g\ \end{pmatrix}=- rac{1}{EG-F^2} egin{pmatrix} G & -F\ -F & E\ \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} e & f\ f & g\ \end{pmatrix}\).

\(a_{11}= rac{Ff-Ge}{EG-F^2},a_{12}= rac{Fg-Gf}{EG-F^2},a_{21}= rac{Fe-Ef}{EG-F^2},a_{22}= rac{Ff-Eg}{EG-F^2}\).

\(K=det\ A= rac{eF-fE}{EG-F^2}\).（注：Just one moment, everybody is doing a little bit od geometry of surfaces should remember by heart this formula.）

\(H=- rac{tr(A)}{2}= rac{1}{2} rac{eG+gE-2fF}{EG-F^2}\).

\(k_i=H\pm\sqrt{H^2-K}\).

The square root, of course, is smooth, as long as what's inside is different from zero. The average is equal to the determinant if and only if the two eigenvalues are the same, so you are at an umbilical point. So outside the umbilical point, \(k_i\) is smooth.\(\square\)

\(X:U\to S\longrightarrow E,F,G,e,f,g \longrightarrow K=\frac{eg-f^2}{EG-F^2},H=\frac{1}{2}\frac{eG+gE-2fE}{EG-F^2},k_i=H\pm\sqrt{H^2-K}\).

Example

1) \(S=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid 2z=x^2+y^2\}\).

\(X(u,v)=(u,v,\frac{u^2+v^2}{2})\).

\(X_u=(1,0,u),X_v=(0,1,v)\).

\(X_{uu}=(0,0,1),X_{uv}=(0,0,0),X_{vv}=(0,0,1)\).

\(N=\frac{X_u\wedge X_v}{|X_u\wedge X_v|}=\frac{(-u,-v,1)}{\sqrt{1+u^2+v^2}}\).

\(E=1+u^2,F=uv,G=1+v^2,EG-F^2=1+v^2+u^2\).

\(e=<-dN(X_u),X_u>=<N,X_{uu}>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+u^2+v^2}},f=<N,X_{uv}>=0,g=<N,X_{vv}>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+u^2+v^2}}\).

\(K(X(u,v))=\frac{1}{(1+v^2+u^2)^2},H(X(u,v))=\frac{2+u^2+v^2}{2(1+v^2+u^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\).

The elliptic paraboloid is all made of elliptic points.

2) Helicoid

\(X(u,v)=(v\cos u,v\sin u,au),a\in\mathbb{R}^*,v\in\mathbb{R},u\in\mathbb{R}\).

\(X_u=(-v\sin u,v\cos u,a),X_v=(\cos u,\sin u,0)\).

\(X_{uu}=(-v\cos u,-v\sin u,0),X_{uv}=(-\sin u,\cos u,0),X_{vv}=(0,0,0)\).

\(N=\frac{(-a\sin u,a\cos u,-v)}{|(-a\sin u,a\cos u,-v)|}=\frac{(-a\sin u,a\cos u,-v)}{\sqrt{a^2+v^2}}\).

\(E=v^2+a^2,F=0,G=1\).

\(e=0,f=\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+v^2}},g=0\).

\(K(X(u,v))=-\frac{a^2}{a^2+v^2}\cdot\frac{1}{a^2+v^2}=-(\frac{a}{a^2+v^2})^2,H(X(u,v))=0\).

It's the first meaningful example of what is called the minimal surface.

The helicoid is completely covered by hyperbolic points.

Definition

\(S\) is a regular surface. \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}. p\in S\) critical point for \(f\).

\((d^2f)_p:T_pS\to\mathbb{R}\quad v\mapsto\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\bigg|_{t=0}(f\circ\alpha)\) is called Hessian of \(f\) at \(p\).

Proposition

If \(p\) is critical, \((d^2f)_p\) is well defined.

1) It is a quadratic form on \(T_pS\).

2) If \(p\) is a local max(resp. min), then \((d^2f)_p\) is semi-definite negative(positive).

3) If \((d^2f)_p\) is negative(positive) definite then \(p\) is a local max(min).

Pf: \(X:U\to S,X(q)=p,q=(a,b)\in U,\alpha(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\subset X(U)\).

\(\beta=X^{-1}\circ\alpha,\beta(t)=(u(t),v(t)),(f\circ\alpha)(t)=(f\circ X)\circ(X^{-1}\circ\alpha)(t)=(f\circ X)(u(t),v(t))\).

\(\frac{d}{dt}(f\circ\alpha)=u'(f\circ X)_u+v'(f\circ X)_v\).

\(\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\bigg|_{t=0}(f\circ \alpha)=u''(f\circ X)_u+u'[u'(f\circ X)_{uu}+v'(f\circ X)_{uv}]+v''(f\circ X)_v+v'[u'(f\circ X)_{uv}+v'(f\circ X)_{vv}](0)\).

We wanted to find a formula for the Hessian where \(\alpha\) dis not appear.

Now, two different \(\alpha\) passing through the same point and with the velocity. Do they need to have the same second derivatives? No. The velocity at the given point cannot determine its acceleration at that point.

\(p\) critical \(\iff\ (f\circ X)_u=(f\circ X)_v(a,b)=0\).

\((d^2 f)_p(v)=u'(0)^2(f\circ X)_{uu}(a,b)+2u'(0)v'(0)(f\circ X)_{uv}(a,b)+v'(0)^2(f\circ X)_{vv}(a,b)\).\(\square\)

Example

1) Height function

\(D=\{a\}^{\perp},|a|=1\).

\(h(p)=<p-p_0,a>\).

\(p\) is critical if \(N(p)=a\).

\((d^2h)_p=\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\bigg|_{t=0}<\alpha(t)-p_0,a>=<\alpha''(0),a>=<\alpha''(0),N(p)>=\mathrm{II}_p(v,v)\).

\(p\) is always a critical point for \(h\) function with \(p=p_0,a=N(p)\).

Theorem

1) If \(K(p)>0,\)i.e. \(p\) is elliptic, then there exists a neighborhood of \(p\in S\) which lies on the same side of the "affine" tangent plane（注：affine tangent plane is the translation of the tangent plane to the point \(p\)） to \(S\) at \(p\). Moreover \(p\) is the only point intersection.

2) If \(K(p)<0\), then in every neighborhood of \(p\) in \(S\), there are points which lies on both sides of the "affine" tangent plane.

Narrative

There is nothing to prove. Because pick a point \(p\), construct the special height function above. The action of this height function is the second fundamental form. So what does it mean that the Gauss curvature is positive? It's telling you exactly that the second fundamental form is strictly definite. Now here, there is the obvious indeterminacy between geometry and analysis because depending on the choice of \(N\), it will be positive or negative. The point is, you fall exactly in the case of the theorem we stated before about the Hessian of a function.

There is no such theorem for \(K(p)=0\).

planar: \(X(u,v)=(u,v,u^3-3v^2u)\) which ia called the "Monkey saddle".

\(X_u=(1,0,3u^2-3v^2),X_v=(0,1,-6uv)\).

\(X_{uu}=(0,0,6u),X_{uv}=(0,0,-6v),X_{vv}=(0,0,-6u)\).

\(N=\frac{(3v^2-3u^2,6vu,1)}{\sqrt{\cdots}}\).

\(E=1+(3u^2-3v^2)^2,e=\frac{6u}{\sqrt{\cdots}},f=\frac{-6v}{\sqrt{\cdots}},g=\frac{-6u}{\sqrt{\cdots}}\).

\(K=\frac{-36u^2+36v^2}{EG-F^2}\).

\(p=X(0,0)\) is planar.

If I draw the affine tangent space, where does the surface lie? On both sides.

Figure: Monkey saddle

\(p\) parabolic: \(z=y^3,z\in (-1,1)\). Draw the line \(z=1\), and rotate this curve around this axis. The points of the picture where \(y=0\) are parabolic. Exercise.

\(p\) critical for \(f\) if \(p_0\in p+\lambda N(p)\) for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).

\((d^2 f)_p(v)=\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\bigg|_{t=0}|\alpha(t)-p_0|^2=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}(2<\alpha'(t),\alpha(t)-p_0>)=2(<\alpha''(0),p-p_0>+|v|^2)=2(|v|^2-\lambda<\alpha''(0),N(p)>)=2(|v|^2-\lambda\mathrm{II}_p(v))\).

Corollary

If \(S\) is compact（注：This topological assumption was there only to guarantee the existence of a minimum or a maximum. If for some other reason you know that there is a point for which your surface has a minimum or a maximum, the corollary will also be true.）, then \(\exists p\in S\) s.t. \(K(p)\ge0\).

Proof

Pf: \(\exists p_1\) min for \(f\) and \(p_2\) max for \(f\).

W.L.O.G. Take the maximum, \((d^2f)_p(v)<0\implies|v|^2<\lambda\mathrm{II}_p(v)\).

This implies what I want if I can argue that \(\lambda\) is positive. I can make \(\lambda\) to be whatever I want, positive or negative. I mean, the value is not free to choose. But I'm free to choose the sign. Because if \(\lambda\) is positive, I'm done. If \(\lambda\) is negative, I reverse \(N\).

At the minimum point, \((d^2f)_p(v)>0\). I seem to get the wrong inequality, but I can make \(\lambda\) to be the one I want and I make it again the good inequality.\(\square\)

Hilbert's theorem: \(S\) oriented, \(k_1\le k_2\) the principal curvatures. Suppose there exists \(p\in S\) s.t. 1) \(K(p)>0\). 2) \(k_1\) has a local min at \(p\). 3) \(k_2\) has a local max at \(p\). Then \(p\) is umbilical.

Pf: Our geometry is kind f \(O_3\) plus translation invariant in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), so just for convenience, we can assume that ou special point.

We can assume \(p=(0,0,0)\) and \(N(p)=(0,0,1)\).

\(e_1=(1,0,0),e_2=(0,1,0)\) are the principal directions at \(p\).

Around \(p\), \(S\) is locally the graph of a differentiable function \(f\).

\(X(u,v)=(u,v,f(u,v)),f(0,0)=0,f_u(0,0)=0,f_v(0,0)=0\).

\(X_u(0,0)=e_1,X_v(0,0)=e_2\).

\(e=\frac{f_{uu}}{\sqrt{1+f_u^2+f_v^2}},f=\frac{f_{uv}}{\sqrt{1+f_u^2+f_v^2}},g=\frac{f_{vv}}{\sqrt{1+f_u^2+f_v^2}}\).（注：These are true on the whole neighborhood. These are general formula for the coefficients of the second fundamental form of the graph, everywhere covered by the graph chart.）

\(f_{uu}(0,0)=k_1(p),f_{uv}(0,0)=0,f_{vv}(0,0)=k_2(p).\)

define: \(\alpha(u)=X(u,0),\beta(v)=X(0,v)\).

\(E_1(v)=\frac{1}{|X_u(0,v)|}X_u(0,v)\in T_{\beta(v)}S\).

\(E_2(v)=\frac{1}{|X_v(u,0)|}X_v(u,0)\in T_{\alpha(u)}S\).

\(h_1(v)=\mathrm{II}_{\beta(v)}(E_1(v),E_1(v)),h_2(u)=\mathrm{II}_{\alpha(u)}(E_2(u))\)

\(h_1(v)=\frac{f_{uu}}{\sqrt{1+f_u^2+f_v^2}(1+f_u^2)}(0,v),h_2(u)=\frac{f_{vv}}{\sqrt{1+f_u^2+f_v^2}(1+f_v^2)}(u,0)\).

\(h_2(0)=\mathrm{II}_p(e_2)=k_2(p)\ge k_2(\alpha(u))\ge\mathrm{II}_{\alpha(u)}(E_2(u))=h_2(u)\).

so 0 is a local max for \(h_2\).

\(h_1(0)=\mathrm{II}_p(e_1)=k_1(p)\le k_1(\beta(v))\le\mathrm{II}_{\beta(v)}(E_1(v))=h_1(v)\).

so 0 is a local min for \(h_1\implies h_2''(0)\le0\le h_1''(0)\).

We got the expressions here and we want to express it in terms of \(f\).

\(h_2'(0)=[-(1+f_v^2)^{-2}2f_vf_{vu}(1+f_u^2+f_v^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_{vv}-\frac{1}{2}(1+f_u^2+f_v^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}}(1+f_v^2)^{-1}f_{vv}(2f_uf_{uu}+2f_vf_{uv})+(1+f_u^2+f_v^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1+f_v^2)^{-1}f_{vvu}](u,0)\).

Recall \(f_{uu}(0,0)=k_1,f_{u,v}(0,0)=0,f_{vv}=k_2,f_u(0,0)=0,f_v(0,0)=0,f(0,0)=0\).

\(h_2''(0)=-f_{vv}(0)f_{uu}f_{uu}(0)+f_{vvuu}(0)\).

\(h_1''(0)=-f_{vv}f_{vv}f_{uu}(0)+f_{vvuu}(0)\).

\(h_2''(0)-h_1''(0)=f_{uu}f_{vv}(0)(f_{vv}(0)-f_{uu}(0))=K(p)(k_2(p)-k_1(p))\le0\).

Now, how is it possible that the product of two numbers is non-positive? Well, if the first one is positive, the second one must be negative. But how is it possible? This is big minus small. So the only possibility is actually they are the same. So this implies the theorem.\(\square\)

Corollary

\(S\) compact and connected and \(K>0\) everywhere. Suppose \(H\) is constant. Then \(S\) is a sphere.（注：In this case, I don't have to be worried about it's a piece of the sphere because it's compact. So it has to be the whole sphere.）

Proof

Pf: Let \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) s.t. \(H(p)\equiv c,\forall p\in S\).

\(c\not\equiv0\) because otherwise \(k_1=-k_2\implies K\le 0\).

Claim: \(S\) is orientable.

Suppose at a given point I choose \(N\) in such a way that \(H\) with this choice of \(N\) is equal to \(c\). I said \(H\) is equal to \(c\), but \(H\) depends on the choice of \(N\). Because otherwise it becomes \(-c\). So if you give me one choice, it's \(c\). If you give me the opposite choice, the only other possibility is \(-N\), I got \(-c\). This forces the normal vector to be one of the two possibilities at every point. There is only one if the two for which \(H\) is equal to \(c\). See, once we observe that \(c\) is non-zero, this determines a choice of \(N\). But this \(N\) has to be globally defined. Because if it stops to be globally defined at some point, it means at some point it has become \(-N\), but then \(H\) would have become \(-c\). The choice of the value of the mean curvature determines a unique normal vector for which that is the value.

Why is it important? If I have an orientable thing, I have a choice of \(N\) everywhere, the Gauss curvature, the principal curvature, the mean curvature, everywhere become globally defined. So this is the advantage of the important thing.

\(\implies k_1,k_2:S\to \mathbb{R}\) are well defined and continuous.

Take \(p\) s.t. \(k_1\) has a local min at \(p\).

\(p\) is a local max for \(k_2\), because \(H\equiv c\).

\(\implies p\) is umbilical.

Actually, if I want to prove that something is a sphere, the only gun I have is to prove that every point is umbilical.

Take \(q\in S,k_2(q)\le k_2(p)=k_1(p)\le k_1(q)\implies k_2(q)=k_1(q)\).

So our surface is covered by umbilical points, every point is umbilical.\(\square\)

Now you can see, this proof is actually very flexible and the most famous. Actually, this was the origin of Hilbert's theorem. But actually, Hilbert himself proved another corollary of his argument, which in some sense, it's even more interesting, and this has passed through history as Hilbert-Liebmann theorem.

Corollary

\(S\) compact and connected. If \(K\) is a constant, then \(S\) is a sphere.

Proof

Pf: \(K\) must be positive.（注：Every compact surface has a point whose Gauss curvature is greater than or equal to zero.）

\(\implies H\) is non-zero everywhere.

\(\implies S\) orientable.

\(k_1,k_2:S\to \mathbb{R}\).

\(p\) min for \(k_1\implies p\) max for \(k_2\implies p\) umbilical \(\implies\) every point is umbilical.\(\square\)

Now, of course, what does a geometer in this sense when studies this subject, you have defined many functions, \(k_1,k_2,H,K\). You would like to classify surfaces by looking at these curvatures. Which are the surfaces for which one or two or three? It's the first question in a general classification theorem.

docs.title: Surfaces of Revolution
docs.text:
Let the generating curve be

\[ (f(v),0,g(v)), f(v)>0, v\in(a,b). \]

The corresponding surface of revolution is parametrized by

\[ X(u,v)=(f(v)\cos u,f(v)\sin u,g(v)), u\in(0,2\pi). \]

Suppose the generating curve is parametrized by arc length, so

\[ f'^2+g'^2=1. \]

Then

\[ X_u=(-f\sin u,f\cos u,0), X_v=(f'\cos u,f'\sin u,g'), \] \[ X_{uu}=(-f\cos u,-f\sin u,0), X_{uv}=(-f'\sin u,f'\cos u,0), X_{vv}=(f''\cos u,f''\sin u,g''). \]

Choose the unit normal field

\[ N=(g'\cos u,g'\sin u,-f'). \]

This field is differentiable throughout the parameter domain, so the surface is orientable.

The coefficients of the first fundamental form are

\[ E=f^2, F=0, G=1, \]

and those of the second fundamental form are

\[ e=-fg', f=0, g=f''g'-f'g''. \] Shape operator

In the basis \(\{X_u,X_v\}\), the matrix of the shape operator is

\[ -dN\longmapsto \begin{pmatrix} E & F\\ F & G \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} e & f\\ f & g \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f^2 & 0\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} -fg' & 0\\ 0 & f''g'-f'g'' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{g'}{f} & 0\\ 0 & f''g'-f'g'' \end{pmatrix}. \]

Since \(f'f''+g'g''=0\),

\[ K=-\frac{g'}{f}(f''g'-f'g'')=-\frac{f''}{f}. \]

Examples

Catenoid

\[ X(u,v)=(a\cosh v\cos u,a\cosh v\sin u,av), a\in\mathbb{R}_+. \]

It is generated by the catenary \((a\cosh v,0,av)\) and satisfies

\[ H\equiv0, K=-\frac{1}{a^2\cosh^4v}. \]

Surface of revolution generated by a tractrix

\[ X(u,v)=(\cosh(av)\cos u,\cosh(av)\sin u,g(v)), \]

where

\[ g(v)=\int_0^v(1-a^2\sinh^2(at))^{\frac12}dt. \]

Here \(K=-a^2\).

docs.title: Ruled Surfaces
docs.text:
A one-parameter family of straight lines \(\{\alpha(t),w(t)\}\) is specified by a differentiable map \(\alpha:I\to\mathbb{R}^3\) and a differentiable nonzero vector field \(w:I\to\mathbb{R}^3\), with \(w(t)\neq0\). The image of

\[ X(t,v)=\alpha(t)+vw(t), v\in\mathbb{R}, \]

is called a ruled surface. The line

\[ L_t=\{\alpha(t)+vw(t):v\in\mathbb{R}\} \]

is called a ruling, and \(\alpha\) is called a directrix.

Examples

0) A plane admits many ruled parametrizations, for example

\[ \alpha(t)=(t,0), w(t)=(0,1), \] \[ \alpha(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), w(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \]

or

\[ \alpha(t)=(0,0), w(t)=(\cos t,\sin t). \]

Thus a set with the desired geometric property generally has no canonical ruled parametrization.

1) Cylinder:

\[ \alpha(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0), w(t)=(0,0,1). \]

More generally, one may take \(\alpha(t)\subset P\) and let \(w(t)\) be constant.

2) Cone: take \(\alpha(t)\subset P\) and require every ruling to pass through a fixed point \(p_0\notin P\).

3) One-sheeted hyperboloid of revolution:

\[ S=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2-z^2=1\}. \]

It has the ruled parametrization

\[ X(s,v)=(\cos s-v\sin s,\sin s+v\cos s,v) =\underbrace{(\cos s,\sin s,0)}_{\alpha} +v\underbrace{(-\sin s,\cos s,1)}_{w}, \]

where \(w=\alpha'+(0,0,1)\).

For various reasons, the image of \(X\) need not be a regular surface everywhere.
