docs.title: Developable Ruled Surfaces
docs.text:
Consider a ruled surface

\[ X(t,v)=\alpha(t)+vw(t). \]

Example: tangent surface to a curve

Taking \(w(t)=\alpha'(t)\) gives

\[ X(t,v)=\alpha(t)+v\alpha'(t). \]

This is the tangent surface of \(\alpha\), one of the types in the classification below.

For a general ruled surface,

\[ X_t=\alpha'+vw', X_v=w, \] \[ X_{tt}=\alpha''+vw'', X_{tv}=w', X_{vv}=0. \]

The following computations apply wherever \(X\) is a regular parametrization. In general, \(X\) may fail to be injective or regular at some points. The unit normal is

\[ N=\frac{X_t\times X_v}{|X_t\times X_v|}. \]

The coefficients of the first fundamental form are

\[ E=|\alpha'+vw'|^2, F=\langle\alpha',w\rangle+v\langle w',w\rangle, G=|w|^2. \]

Write the scalar triple product as

\[ (a,b,c)=\langle a,b\times c\rangle. \]

For the second fundamental form,

\[ f=\frac{(\alpha',w,w')}{|\alpha'\times w+vw'\times w|}, g=0. \]

Hence

\[ K=-\frac{(\alpha',w,w')^2}{|\alpha'\times w+vw'\times w|^2}\frac{1}{EG-F^2}\leq0, \]

and \(K\equiv0\) if and only if \((\alpha',w,w')=0\). Without loss of generality, take \(|w|=1\); then \(\langle w,w'\rangle=0\).

Definition

A ruled surface is called developable if

\[ (\alpha',w,w')=0. \]

We now classify developable surfaces.

  1. If \(w\times w'=0\), then \(w'(t)=\lambda(t)w(t)\). Since
\[ 0=\langle w,w'\rangle=\lambda\langle w,w\rangle=\lambda, \]

we obtain \(w'\equiv0\) and \(w(t)=w_0\), so the surface is a cylinder.

  1. If \(w\times w'\neq0\), then \(\{\alpha',w,w'\}\) is linearly dependent, so
\[ \alpha'(t)=\lambda(t)w(t)+\mu(t)w'(t). \]

Set

\[ \widetilde{\alpha}(t)=\alpha(t)-\mu(t)w(t). \]

Then

\[ \widetilde{\alpha}'=\alpha'-\mu'w-\mu w'=(\lambda-\mu')w. \]

If \(\widetilde{\alpha}'\equiv0\), then \(\widetilde{\alpha}\equiv\alpha_0\), and therefore

\[ \alpha(t)=\alpha_0+\mu(t)w(t), \]

and

\[ X(t,v)=\alpha_0+(\mu(t)+v)w(t), \]

so the surface is a cone.

If \(\widetilde{\alpha}'\neq0\), then the identity above gives

\[ X(t,v)=\widetilde{\alpha}(t)+(\mu(t)+v)w(t) =\widetilde{\alpha}(t)+\frac{\mu(t)+v}{\lambda(t)-\mu'(t)}\widetilde{\alpha}'(t), \]

so the surface is the tangent surface of \(\widetilde{\alpha}\).

Cylinders, cones, and tangent surfaces therefore form a large class of surfaces with identically zero Gauss curvature. This brings us closer to the geometric meaning of Gauss curvature: curvature should distinguish flat surfaces from curved ones.

docs.title: The First Fundamental Form and Area
docs.text:
The length of a curve \(\alpha\) is

\[ L(\alpha)=\int|\alpha'(t)|dt. \]

Suppose \(\alpha=X\circ\beta\), where \(\beta(t)=(u(t),v(t))\). Then

\[ |\alpha'(t)|=\left(u'^2E+2u'v'F+v'^2G\right)^{\frac12}, \]

whereas the Euclidean length of \(\beta\) in the parameter domain is

\[ L(\beta)=\int\left(u'^2+v'^2\right)^{\frac12}dt. \]

Thus the first fundamental form measures exactly how \(X\) distorts lengths from the coordinate domain. Moreover,

\[ |X_u\times X_v|=(EG-F^2)^{\frac12}. \]

Definition

If \(V\) lies in the parameter domain, then

\[ \operatorname{Area}(X(V))=\int_V(EG-F^2)^{\frac12}dudv. \]

If two charts cover the same region, does its area depend on the chart? This is an exercise.

The first fundamental form therefore controls two basic geometric quantities on a surface: lengths of curves and areas of regions.

docs.title: Minimal Surfaces and Normal Variations
docs.text:
When studying surfaces with zero Gauss curvature, we considered ruled surfaces. Surfaces with zero mean curvature lead instead to minimal surfaces.

Definition

A regular surface is called minimal if \(H\equiv0\).

Let \(X:U\to S\) be a local chart, let \(D\subset U\) be a bounded domain, and let \(h:\overline D\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. The normal variation of \(X(\overline D)\) determined by \(h\) is

\[ \varphi:\overline D\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to\mathbb{R}^3, \] \[ \varphi(u,v,t)=X(u,v)+th(u,v)N(u,v). \]

For \(t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\), write

\[ X^t(u,v)=\varphi(u,v,t). \]

Then

\[ X_u^t=X_u+th_uN+thN_u, X_v^t=X_v+th_vN+thN_v. \]

Keeping terms through first order in \(t\) gives

\[ E^t=E-2the+O(t^2), F^t=F-2thf+O(t^2), G^t=G-2thg+O(t^2). \]

Therefore

\[ E^tG^t-(F^t)^2 =EG-F^2-2th(Eg-2Ff+Ge)+O(t^2) =(EG-F^2)(1-4thH)+O(t^2). \]

It follows that

\[ \operatorname{Area}(X^t(\overline D)) =\int_{\overline D}(EG-F^2)^{\frac12}(1-4thH)^{\frac12}dudv+O(t^2), \]

and

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}\operatorname{Area}(X^t(\overline D)) =-\int_{\overline D}2hH(EG-F^2)^{\frac12}dudv. \]

If \(X\) is minimal, the first variation of area vanishes for every normal variation. Conversely, if

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}\operatorname{Area}(X^t(\overline D))=0 \]

for every \(h\), then \(H\equiv0\). This is the variational characterization of minimal surfaces.

The plane is a minimal surface. The catenoid and helicoid are also minimal surfaces.

On the word ‘minimal’

The name “minimal surface” can be misleading: the calculation above shows that the surface is a critical point of the area functional, not necessarily a minimum. Establishing a local minimum would require computing the second variation and proving that it is nonnegative. In this theory, “minimal” therefore means critical before it means minimizing.

Given a closed curve as boundary, does there exist a minimal surface spanning it? This is the starting point of the Plateau problem.

Physical model

If area is interpreted as energy, one is naturally led to soap films. Soap films are the standard physical model for minimal-surface theory.

docs.title: Lecture 13
docs.text:
Chapter: The Intrinsic Geometry of Surfaces

Whenever a class of objects is defined in mathematics, one naturally hopes to classify them up to some equivalence relation. Introducing the objects also implicitly introduces a notion of equivalence among them.

docs.title: Isometries
docs.text:
Definition

Surfaces \(S\) and \(\widetilde S\) are isometric if there is a diffeomorphism \(f:S\to\widetilde S\) that maps every curve on \(S\) to a curve of the same length on \(\widetilde S\). Such a map \(f\) is called an isometry.

A patch of a surface is the image of a local chart \(X:U\to S\).

Theorem

Two patches of surfaces \(S\) and \(\widetilde S\) are isometric if and only if they can be parametrized by

\[ X:U\to S, \widetilde X:U\to\widetilde S, \]

so that their first fundamental forms coincide.

Proof

Proof. If the first fundamental forms coincide, every curve has images of the same length in the two patches, so the patches are isometric.

Conversely, let \(f:S\to\widetilde S\) be an isometry. Start with any local chart \(X:U\to S\) covering the patch in \(S\), and define

\[ \widetilde X=f\circ X:U\to\widetilde S. \]

Since \(f\) is an isometry, every curve \((u(t),v(t))\) in \(U\), with \(t\in[0,\varepsilon]\), satisfies

\[ \int_0^{\varepsilon}\left(Eu'^2+2Fu'v'+Gv'^2\right)^{\frac12}dt =\int_0^{\varepsilon}\left(\widetilde Eu'^2+2\widetilde Fu'v'+\widetilde Gv'^2\right)^{\frac12}dt. \]

Fix \((u_0,v_0)\in U\). Taking curves in the two coordinate directions and in the diagonal direction gives

\[ \begin{aligned} (u_0+t,v_0)&: E(u_0,v_0)=\widetilde E(u_0,v_0),\\ (u_0,v_0+t)&: G(u_0,v_0)=\widetilde G(u_0,v_0),\\ (u_0+t,v_0+t)&: F(u_0,v_0)=\widetilde F(u_0,v_0). \end{aligned} \]

Here we used

\[ \lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_0^\varepsilon h(t)dt=h(0). \]

Thus the first fundamental forms coincide. \(\square\)

Examples

  1. A part of the plane is isometric to a part of a cylinder. The entire plane and the entire cylinder are not isometric; they are not even homeomorphic.

  2. Consider the cone

\[ C=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2=z^2\}. \]

For

\[ (u,v)\in(0,+\infty)\times(0,\sqrt2\pi), \]

take

\[ X(u,v)=\left(\frac{u}{\sqrt2}\cos(v\sqrt2),\frac{u}{\sqrt2}\sin(v\sqrt2),\frac{u}{\sqrt2}\right), \] \[ \widetilde X(u,v)=(u\cos v,u\sin v,0). \]

These two parametrizations have the same first fundamental form.

Figure: Corresponding regions on a cone and the plane

docs.title: Conformal and Area-Preserving Parametrizations
docs.text:
Angle information in the first fundamental form

The first fundamental form measures not only the lengths of tangent vectors but also the angles between them. Curve length is obtained by integrating the norm of the tangent vector, while the full first fundamental form also gives inner products between different directions and therefore contains additional information.

Definition

Let \(X:U\to S\) be a local parametrization.

  1. The map \(X\) is conformal if it preserves the angles between intersecting curves.

  2. The map \(X\) is area preserving if

\[ \operatorname{Area}(X(V))=\operatorname{Area}(V) \]

for every relatively compact set \(V\Subset U\).

Proposition

  1. \(X\) is conformal if and only if \(E=G\) and \(F=0\).

  2. \(X\) is area preserving if and only if \(EG-F^2=1\).

Proof

Proof. For two curves in the parameter domain, the angle \(\theta\) between their tangent vectors satisfies

\[ \cos\theta= \frac{u'\widetilde u'+v'\widetilde v'} {\sqrt{u'^2+v'^2}\sqrt{\widetilde u'^2+\widetilde v'^2}}. \]

The tangent vectors to their images are

\[ \xi=u'X_u+v'X_v, \widetilde\xi=\widetilde u'X_u+\widetilde v'X_v, \]

and the angle \(\varphi\) between them satisfies

\[ \cos\varphi= \frac{u'\widetilde u'E+(u'\widetilde v'+v'\widetilde u')F+v'\widetilde v'G} {\sqrt{u'^2E+2u'v'F+v'^2G}\sqrt{\widetilde u'^2E+2\widetilde u'\widetilde v'F+\widetilde v'^2G}}. \]

First take curves in the two coordinate directions:

\[ \begin{aligned} (u(t),v(t))&=(t,0),\\ (\widetilde u(t),\widetilde v(t))&=(0,t). \end{aligned} \]

Angle preservation gives \(F=0\). Next take curves in the directions \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\):

\[ \begin{aligned} (u(t),v(t))&=(t,t),\\ (\widetilde u(t),\widetilde v(t))&=(t,-t). \end{aligned} \]

This gives \(E=G\). The converse follows by substituting these conditions into the formula for \(\cos\varphi\).

The second assertion follows immediately from the area formula

\[ \operatorname{Area}(X(V))=\int_V\sqrt{EG-F^2}dudv. \]

\(\square\)

Example: stereographic projection

Stereographic projection of the unit sphere can be written as the conformal parametrization

\[ \pi:\mathbb{R}^2\to S^2, \] \[ (x,y)\longmapsto \left( \frac{2x}{1+x^2+y^2}, \frac{2y}{1+x^2+y^2}, \frac{-1+x^2+y^2}{1+x^2+y^2} \right). \]

There is no isometry between a piece of the plane and a piece of the sphere. Gauss established this by proving one of the most important theorems in the theory of surfaces.

docs.title: Gauss’s Theorema Egregium
docs.text:
Theorem

Gauss curvature is invariant under isometries. More precisely, if \(f:S\to S'\) is an isometry and \(K,K'\) are the Gauss curvatures of the two surfaces, then

\[ K(p)=K'(f(p)) \]

for every \(p\in S\).

Proof outline

Take a local chart \(X:U\to S\). Gauss curvature is initially expressed using both fundamental forms:

\[ K=\frac{eg-f^2}{EG-F^2}. \]

The strategy is to show that \(eg-f^2\) can be expressed in terms of \(E,F,G\) and their derivatives. Gauss curvature then depends only on the first fundamental form. Since isometric patches have the same first fundamental form, they must have the same Gauss curvature.

Orthonormalize \(\{X_u,X_v\}\) to obtain \(\{e_1,e_2\}\). Write

\[ e_{i,u}=\frac{\partial e_i}{\partial u}, e_{i,v}=\frac{\partial e_i}{\partial v}. \]

There are functions \(\alpha_i,\lambda_i,\mu_i\) such that

\[ \begin{aligned} e_{1,u}&=\alpha_1e_2+\lambda_1N,\\ e_{1,v}&=\alpha_2e_2+\lambda_2N,\\ e_{2,u}&=-\alpha_1e_1+\mu_1N,\\ e_{2,v}&=-\alpha_2e_1+\mu_2N. \end{aligned} \]

Here we use

\[ 0=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle \implies \langle e_{1,u},e_2\rangle+\langle e_1,e_{2,u}\rangle=0. \]

Claim:

\[ \begin{aligned} \langle e_{1,u},e_{2,v}\rangle-\langle e_{1,v},e_{2,u}\rangle &=\lambda_1\mu_2-\lambda_2\mu_1\\ &=\frac{\partial\alpha_1}{\partial v}-\frac{\partial\alpha_2}{\partial u}\\ &=\frac{eg-f^2}{\sqrt{EG-F^2}}. \end{aligned} \]

For the middle equality,

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\alpha_1}{\partial v}-\frac{\partial\alpha_2}{\partial u} &=-\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\langle e_{2,u},e_1\rangle +\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\langle e_{2,v},e_1\rangle\\ &=-\langle e_{2,uv},e_1\rangle-\langle e_{2,u},e_{1,v}\rangle +\langle e_{2,vu},e_1\rangle+\langle e_{2,v},e_{1,u}\rangle\\ &=\langle e_{1,u},e_{2,v}\rangle-\langle e_{1,v},e_{2,u}\rangle. \end{aligned} \]

On the other hand,

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{eg-f^2}{\sqrt{EG-F^2}} &=\langle N_u\times N_v,N\rangle\\ &=\langle N_u\times N_v,e_1\times e_2\rangle\\ &=\langle N_u,e_1\rangle\langle N_v,e_2\rangle -\langle N_u,e_2\rangle\langle N_v,e_1\rangle\\ &=\langle N,e_{1,u}\rangle\langle N,e_{2,v}\rangle -\langle N,e_{2,u}\rangle\langle N,e_{1,v}\rangle\\ &=\lambda_1\mu_2-\mu_1\lambda_2. \end{aligned} \]

It remains to prove that \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) are determined by the first fundamental form.

docs.title: Lecture 14
docs.text: Chapter: The Intrinsic Geometry of Surfaces

docs.title: Proof of Gauss’s Theorema Egregium, Continued
docs.text:
Orthonormalize \(\{X_u,X_v\}\) to obtain \(\{e_1,e_2\}\):

\[ \{X_u,X_v\}\xrightarrow{\text{O.N.}}\{e_1,e_2\}. \]

Recall that

\[ \begin{aligned} e_{1,u}&=\alpha_1e_2+\lambda_1N,\\ e_{1,v}&=\alpha_2e_2+\lambda_2N,\\ e_{2,u}&=-\alpha_1e_1+\mu_1N,\\ e_{2,v}&=-\alpha_2e_1+\mu_2N. \end{aligned} \]

The previous lecture established that

\[ \begin{aligned} \langle e_{1,u},e_{2,v}\rangle-\langle e_{1,v},e_{2,u}\rangle &=\lambda_1\mu_2-\lambda_2\mu_1\\ &=\frac{\partial\alpha_1}{\partial v}-\frac{\partial\alpha_2}{\partial u}\\ &=\frac{eg-f^2}{\sqrt{EG-F^2}}. \end{aligned} \]

The last equality follows from

\[ \begin{aligned} \langle N_u\times N_v,N\rangle &=\frac{\langle N_u\times N_v,X_u\times X_v\rangle}{|X_u\times X_v|}\\ &=\frac{\langle N_u,X_u\rangle\langle N_v,X_v\rangle -\langle N_u,X_v\rangle\langle N_v,X_u\rangle}{\sqrt{EG-F^2}}\\ &=\frac{eg-f^2}{\sqrt{EG-F^2}}. \end{aligned} \]

Equivalently, in the orthonormal frame,

\[ \begin{aligned} \langle N_u\times N_v,N\rangle &=\langle N_u\times N_v,e_1\times e_2\rangle\\ &=\langle N_u,e_1\rangle\langle N_v,e_2\rangle -\langle N_u,e_2\rangle\langle N_v,e_1\rangle\\ &=\langle N,e_{1,u}\rangle\langle N,e_{2,v}\rangle -\langle N,e_{2,u}\rangle\langle N,e_{1,v}\rangle\\ &=\lambda_1\mu_2-\lambda_2\mu_1. \end{aligned} \]

It remains to prove that \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) can be expressed in terms of \(E,F,G\) and their derivatives. Set

\[ \Delta=EG-F^2, \]

and take

\[ \begin{aligned} e_1&=aX_u,& a&=E^{-1/2},\\ e_2&=bX_u+cX_v,& b&=-\frac{F}{\sqrt{E}\sqrt{\Delta}},& c&=\frac{\sqrt E}{\sqrt\Delta}. \end{aligned} \]

Using

\[ \langle X_{uu},X_u\rangle=\frac12E_u, \] \[ \langle X_{uu},X_v\rangle=F_u-\frac12E_v, \]

we obtain

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha_1 &=\langle e_{1,u},e_2\rangle\\ &=a\langle X_{uu},e_2\rangle+a_u\langle X_u,e_2\rangle\\ &=a\left(b\langle X_{uu},X_u\rangle+c\langle X_{uu},X_v\rangle\right)\\ &=\frac{ab}{2}E_u+ac\left(F_u-\frac12E_v\right). \end{aligned} \]

Similarly,

\[ \alpha_2 =\langle e_{1,v},e_2\rangle =\frac{ab}{2}E_v+\frac{ac}{2}G_u. \]

Thus \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) depend only on the first fundamental form, completing the proof of Gauss’s Theorema Egregium. \(\square\)

In particular, if \(F=0\), then

\[ K=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{EG}} \left[ \frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{EG}}G_u\right) +\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{EG}}E_v\right) \right]. \]

If, in addition, \(E=1\), then

\[ K=-G^{-\frac12}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial u^2}\left(G^{\frac12}\right). \]

docs.title: Geodesics
docs.text:
Given two points on a surface, which curve of shortest length joins them? Since we can measure curve lengths on any surface, we can ask this question intrinsically.

Definition

  1. A smooth family of curves on \(S\) is a smooth map
\[ \Gamma:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times[a,b]\to S. \]

For fixed \(s\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\), write

\[ \Gamma(s,t)=\gamma_s(t) \]

and regard this as a curve in the variable \(t\).

  1. A smooth curve \(\gamma:[a,b]\to S\) is a geodesic if every smooth family satisfying
\[ \gamma_0=\gamma, \gamma_s(a)=\gamma(a), \gamma_s(b)=\gamma(b) \]

also satisfies

\[ \frac{d}{ds}\bigg|_{s=0}L_a^b(\gamma_s)=0. \]

In other words, a geodesic is a critical point of the length functional.

Let

\[ \gamma_s(t)=X(u(s,t),v(s,t)), \]

and write

\[ \dot u=\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}, \dot v=\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}. \]

Set

\[ R=E\dot u^2+2F\dot u\dot v+G\dot v^2. \]

This is the squared norm of the tangent vector to the curve, so

\[ L(\gamma_s)=\int_a^bR^{\frac12}dt, \] \[ \frac{d}{ds}L(\gamma_s)=\frac12\int_a^bR^{-\frac12}\frac{\partial R}{\partial s}dt. \]

A direct computation gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial R}{\partial s} &=\left(E_u\dot u^2+2F_u\dot u\dot v+G_u\dot v^2\right)u_s\\ &\mathrel{+}\left(E_v\dot u^2+2F_v\dot u\dot v+G_v\dot v^2\right)v_s\\ &\mathrel{+}2(E\dot u+F\dot v)\dot u_s +2(F\dot u+G\dot v)\dot v_s. \end{aligned} \]

Integrating the last two terms by parts and using the fixed-endpoint conditions

\[ u_s(s,a)=v_s(s,a)=u_s(s,b)=v_s(s,b)=0, \]

gives

\[ \frac{dL(\gamma_s)}{ds}\bigg|_{s=0} =\int_a^b(Pu_s+Qv_s)dt, \]

where

\[ P=\frac12R^{-\frac12}\left(E_u\dot u^2+2F_u\dot u\dot v+G_u\dot v^2\right) -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(R^{-\frac12}(E\dot u+F\dot v)\right), \] \[ Q=\frac12R^{-\frac12}\left(E_v\dot u^2+2F_v\dot u\dot v+G_v\dot v^2\right) -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(R^{-\frac12}(F\dot u+G\dot v)\right). \]

The variation fields \(u_s\) and \(v_s\) can be chosen arbitrarily, so

\[ \gamma\text{ is a geodesic}\iff P=Q=0. \]

Corollary

If \(\gamma\) is parametrized by arc length, then \(R=1\), and \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if

\[ \frac{d}{dt}(E\dot u+F\dot v) =\frac12\left(E_u\dot u^2+2F_u\dot u\dot v+G_u\dot v^2\right), \] \[ \frac{d}{dt}(F\dot u+G\dot v) =\frac12\left(E_v\dot u^2+2F_v\dot u\dot v+G_v\dot v^2\right). \]

Whether a curve is a geodesic depends only on the first fundamental form. Consequently, an isometry maps geodesics to geodesics.

Geometric interpretation: \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if its acceleration is normal to the surface at every point, or equivalently if its tangential component vanishes. Indeed,

\[ \gamma(t)=X(u(t),v(t)), \gamma'(t)=\dot uX_u+\dot vX_v, \]

and the conditions

\[ \left\langle\frac{d}{dt}(\dot uX_u+\dot vX_v),X_u\right\rangle=0, \] \[ \left\langle\frac{d}{dt}(\dot uX_u+\dot vX_v),X_v\right\rangle=0 \]

are exactly the geodesic equations above. Verifying this is an exercise.

Intrinsic and extrinsic geometry

Intrinsic geometry can be understood as the geometry measurable by an observer living on the surface. Quantities that depend only on the first fundamental form are intrinsic; they can be recovered from lengths and angles within the surface. Quantities involving the normal vector or the second fundamental form are extrinsic because they require knowledge of how the surface sits in the surrounding three-dimensional space. Geodesics are intrinsic objects because they are determined entirely by the length functional, or equivalently by the first fundamental form.

docs.title: Lecture 15
docs.text:
Chapter: The Intrinsic Geometry of Surfaces

Let \(\gamma\) be parametrized by arc length. From the previous lecture,

\[ \gamma\text{ is a geodesic} \iff \begin{cases} \dfrac{d}{dt}(E\dot u+F\dot v)=\dfrac12\left(E_u\dot u^2+2F_u\dot u\dot v+G_u\dot v^2\right),\\ \dfrac{d}{dt}(F\dot u+G\dot v)=\dfrac12\left(E_v\dot u^2+2F_v\dot u\dot v+G_v\dot v^2\right). \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Existence and Uniqueness of Geodesics
docs.text:
Theorem

For every \(p\in S\) and every \(w\in T_pS\), there is a unique local geodesic \(\gamma\) such that

\[ \gamma(0)=p, \gamma'(0)=w. \]

Proof outline. The geodesic equations can be reduced to a system of the form

\[ \begin{cases} \ddot u=A(u,v,\dot u,\dot v),\\ \ddot v=B(u,v,\dot u,\dot v). \end{cases} \]

This is an initial-value problem for a second-order system of ordinary differential equations. The standard local existence and uniqueness theorem gives a unique solution on some interval \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\).

Examples

  1. If \(S\) is the plane, then
\[ \ddot u=\ddot v=0. \]

Thus straight lines are geodesics in the plane, and they are the only geodesics.

  1. Consider the punctured plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\). Starting from any point and initial direction, a geodesic agrees with the corresponding straight line until it reaches the missing origin. If the line points toward the origin, the solution is defined only up to that point because the origin does not belong to the surface.

docs.title: Geodesics on Surfaces of Revolution
docs.text:
Consider the surface of revolution

\[ X(u,v)=(f(v)\cos u,f(v)\sin u,g(v)), \]

where \(v\in(a,b)\), \(u\in(0,2\pi)\), and \(f>0\). The coefficients of the first fundamental form are

\[ E=f^2, F=0, G=f'^2+g'^2. \]

The geodesic equations become

\[ \begin{cases} \dfrac{d}{dt}(f^2\dot u)=0,\\ \dfrac{d}{dt}(G\dot v)=ff'\dot u^2+(f'f''+g'g'')\dot v^2. \end{cases} \]

Expanding gives

\[ \begin{cases} 2ff'\dot u\dot v+f^2\ddot u=0,\\ 2(f'f''+g'g'')\dot v^2+(f'^2+g'^2)\ddot v =ff'\dot u^2+(f'f''+g'g'')\dot v^2, \end{cases} \]

or equivalently

\[ \begin{cases} \ddot u+2\dfrac{f'}{f}\dot u\dot v=0,\\ \ddot v-\dfrac{ff'}{f'^2+g'^2}\dot u^2 +\dfrac{f'f''+g'g''}{f'^2+g'^2}\dot v^2=0. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Meridians
docs.text:
Let \(u(t)=u_0\). The arc-length condition gives

\[ 1=|\dot\gamma|^2=G\dot v^2, \]

so

\[ \dot v^2=\frac{1}{f'^2+g'^2}. \]

Differentiating yields

\[ 2\dot v\ddot v =-\frac{2(f'f''+g'g'')}{(f'^2+g'^2)^2}\dot v. \]

This is exactly the second geodesic equation, while the first is automatic because \(\dot u=0\). Hence every meridian is a geodesic.

docs.title: Parallels
docs.text:
Let \(v(t)=v_0\). The geodesic equations reduce to

\[ \begin{cases} \ddot u=0,\\ -\dfrac{ff'}{f'^2+g'^2}\dot u^2=0. \end{cases} \]

The arc-length condition is

\[ 1=|\dot\gamma|^2=f^2\dot u^2, \]

so

\[ \dot u^2=\frac{1}{f^2}. \]

Since \(f>0\), the parallel \(v=v_0\) is a geodesic if and only if

\[ f'(v_0)=0. \]

docs.title: Geodesic Coordinates
docs.text:
Geodesics can be used to construct special coordinates on any surface. Let \(\gamma(v)\) be an arc-length-parametrized geodesic with \(\gamma(0)=p\). For sufficiently small \(v\), let \(\gamma_v(u)\) be the unit-speed geodesic through \(\gamma(v)\) whose initial velocity is orthogonal to \(\gamma'(v)\), and define

\[ X(u,v)=\gamma_v(u), |u|<\delta. \]

For sufficiently small \(u\), this map has rank \(2\) and therefore defines a local chart. Such a chart is called geodesic coordinates.

Proposition

In geodesic coordinates,

\[ E=1, F=0, \]

while \(G\) is unrestricted.

Proof. For each fixed \(v\), the curve \(u\mapsto X(u,v)\) is a unit-speed geodesic, so \(E=1\). At \(u=0\), the construction makes \(X_u\) orthogonal to \(X_v\), hence \(F(0,v)=0\).

Along a coordinate curve in the \(u\)-direction, take \(\dot u=1\) and \(\dot v=0\). The second geodesic equation gives

\[ F_u=\frac12E_v=0. \]

Therefore \(F(u,v)=F(0,v)=0\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Local Classification of Surfaces with Constant Gauss Curvature
docs.text:
Theorem

  1. A surface with identically zero Gauss curvature is locally isometric to the plane.

  2. A surface with positive constant Gauss curvature is locally isometric to a sphere of the corresponding radius.

  3. A surface with negative constant Gauss curvature is locally isometric to a pseudosphere of the same curvature.

Why the conclusion is only local

The word “locally” cannot simply be removed from these statements. Local isometry does not determine global topology: for example, the cylinder and the plane are locally isometric but are not even homeomorphic. Strengthening local isometry to global isometry requires additional control of the surface’s global topology.

Proof. In geodesic coordinates,

\[ K=-G^{-\frac12}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial u^2}\left(G^{\frac12}\right). \]

Set \(h=G^{\frac12}\). Along the initial geodesic \(u=0\), the construction gives

\[ h(0,v)=1, h_u(0,v)=0. \]
  1. If \(K=0\), then
\[ h_{uu}=0. \]

Hence

\[ h(u,v)=A(v)u+B(v). \]

The initial conditions give \(A(v)=0\) and \(B(v)=1\), so \(G=1\). The first fundamental form is therefore

\[ du^2+dv^2, \]

the same as that of the plane. Thus the surface is locally isometric to the plane.

  1. If \(K=a^2>0\), then
\[ h_{uu}+a^2h=0. \]

The initial conditions give

\[ h(u,v)=\cos(au), \]

and hence

\[ G(u,v)=\cos^2(au). \]

These are the coefficients of the first fundamental form of a sphere of radius \(1/a\) in corresponding geodesic coordinates. The surface is therefore locally isometric to that sphere.

  1. If \(K=-a^2<0\), then
\[ h_{uu}-a^2h=0. \]

The initial conditions give

\[ h(u,v)=\cosh(au), G(u,v)=\cosh^2(au). \]

This is the same local first fundamental form as the corresponding model of constant negative curvature, so the surface is locally isometric to a pseudosphere. \(\square\)

Gauss curvature is an intrinsic property. In fact, among the principal curvatures, mean curvature, and Gauss curvature, only Gauss curvature is intrinsic.

\(n^T = \text{projection of } n \text{ on } T_p S\), \(|n^T| = |k_g|\). \(k_g\) is called the geodesic curvature of \(\gamma\) at \(p\).

Geodesic iff \(k_g = 0\).

Theorem

Let \(\gamma\) be a smooth closed simple curve on a patch of a surface \(S\), enclosing a region \(R\). Then

\[ \int_\gamma k_g \, ds = 2\pi - \int_R K \, dA. \]

注

Write \(dA\) to mean the measure induced on the surface by the first fundamental form. It's the \(\sqrt{EG - F^2} du dv\).

Pf: Assume \(\gamma\) p.a.l. and \(X: V \to \mathbb{R}^3\) is the patch which contains everything. Choose vector fields \(e_1, e_2\) s.t. \(\{e_1, e_2\}(p)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(T_p S\) and restrict them to \(\gamma\).

\[ e_i' = \frac{d}{ds} e_i \]

Let \(\theta(s)\) be the angle between \(\gamma'\) and \(e_1\), \(\gamma' = \cos\theta e_1 + \sin\theta e_2\). Define \(\eta = N \times \gamma'\), \(\eta = -\sin\theta e_1 + \cos\theta e_2\).

\[ \gamma'' = \theta' \eta + \cos\theta e_1' + \sin\theta e_2' \] Narrative

So the geodesic curvature is \(k_g = \langle \eta, \gamma'' \rangle = \theta' + \langle \cos\theta e_1' + \sin\theta e_2', -\sin\theta e_1 + \cos\theta e_2 \rangle（注：\)\langle e_1, e_2 \rangle = 0 \implies \langle e_1', e_2 \rangle + \langle e_1, e_2' \rangle = 0\(.） = \theta' - \langle e_1, e_2' \rangle\).

\[ \int \theta' = 2\pi, \quad I = \int_\gamma \langle e_1, e_2' \rangle, \quad \beta = (u(t), v(t)), \quad \gamma = X \circ \beta \] \[ e_2' = u' e_{2,u} + v' e_{2,v} \]

Define \(P = \langle e_1, e_{2,u} \rangle\), \(Q = \langle e_1, e_{2,v} \rangle\).

\[ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial u} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial v} = \langle e_{1,u}, e_{2,v} \rangle - \langle e_{1,v}, e_{2,u} \rangle \stackrel{\text{Theorema Egregium}}{=} \frac{eg - f^2}{(EG - F^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}} \]

Apply Green's formula,

\[ \int_\gamma k_g \, ds = 2\pi - I = 2\pi - \int_\beta (P dv + Q du) \] \[ = 2\pi - \int_R \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial u} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial v} \right) du dv = 2\pi - \int_R \frac{eg - f^2}{EG - F^2} dA = 2\pi - \int_R K \, dA. \]

\(\square\)

If \(\gamma\) is piece-wise smooth,

\[ \int \theta' = 2\pi - \sum \delta_i, \quad \delta_i \text{ is exterior angles} \]

So if \(\alpha_i = \pi - \delta_i\) the interior angle.

Theorem

\(\gamma\) piece-wise smooth simple closed curve with \(n\)-sides with internal angles \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\),

\[ \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i = (n-2)\pi + \int_\gamma k_g \, ds + \int_R K \, dA. \]

注

The first correction comes from the fact that edges are not segments. The second correction comes from the fact that you are on a surface.

Narrative

If a surface contains a piece of a stratum, a segment, this segment has to be a geodesic. A geodesic is a critical point of length. A segment is a critical, in fact, in this case, it's a minimum of length, automatically. Because if it wasn't a minimum on a surface, it would not be a minimum even in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). So in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), you would have a curve which joins the two vertices of the segment with less length, which is impossible.

Definition

A subdivision of a compact surface \(S\) is a partition into three subsets \(S_0, S_1, S_2\) s.t.

1) \(S_0 = \{p_1, \dots, p_v\}\), \(p_i\) are called vertices.

2) \(S_1\) is a disjoint union of subsets \(e_1, \dots, e_E \subset S\). For each \(e_i\) there are \(p, q \in S_0\) and continuous injections \(f_i: [0,1] \to S\) s.t. \(f_i(0) = p\), \(f_i(1) = q\) and \(f_i|_{(0,1)}\) subjects onto \(e_i\). These \(e_i\) are called edges.

3) \(S_2\) disjoint union of open subsets \(f_1, \dots, f_F\) each of which is homeomorphic to a disc. These \(f_j\) are called faces.

Definition

Euler characteristic of \(S\) relative to the subdivision \(\mathcal{P}\) is \(\chi(S, \mathcal{P}) = V - E + F\).

This number does not depend on the subdivision but only on the surface.

Theorem

\(\chi(S, \mathcal{P}) = \chi(S, \mathcal{P}')\quad\) \(\forall \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{P}'\) subdivision.

Theorem

Every compact surface has one subdivision.

\(\chi(S, \mathcal{P})\) is a number \(\chi(S)\) which depends only on \(S\) and it's called just the Euler characteristic of the surface.

Two homeomorphic surfaces have the same Euler characteristic.

The sphere is the only compact surface up to homeomorphism with Euler characteristic 2.

Two surfaces with the same Euler characteristic are indeed homeomorphic if they are orientable.

\(\chi(S^1 \times S^1) = 0\). \(S^1 \times S^1\) is the only compact orientable surface with zero Euler characteristic.

Theorem

\(S\) be a compact smooth surface. Then

\[ \int_S K \, dA = 2\pi \chi(S). \]

Theorem

Narrative

Be careful, it's not true that if two compact surfaces, without any assumption on orientability, have the same Euler characteristic, then they are homeomorphic. It is possible to have one orientable surface with the same Euler characteristic to a non-orientable surface.

You can prove that the Euler characteristic of the surface with \(g\)-holes is \(2 - 2g\).

By combining the classification of surfaces with the Gauss–Bonnet theorem, one can in principle prove that the Earth is homeomorphic to a sphere.

These two surfaces are locally isometric.

About the converse to the Theorema Egregium:

If for two surfaces, there is in principle a map which sends a point of a given curvature to a point of the same curvature. Is this map isometric? The answer is no.

\[ X(u,v) = \bigl(u\cos v,\, u\sin v,\, \log u\bigr) \] \[ Y(u,v) = \bigl(u\cos v,\, u\sin v,\, v\bigr) \] \[ X_u = \bigl(\cos v,\, \sin v,\, \tfrac{1}{u}\bigr),\quad X_v = \bigl(-u\sin v,\, u\cos v,\, 0\bigr) \] \[ N = \frac{(-\cos v,\, -\sin v,\, u)}{\sqrt{1+u^2}} \] \[ X_{uu} = \bigl(0,0,\, -\tfrac{1}{u^2}\bigr),\quad X_{uv} = \bigl(-\sin v,\, \cos v,\, 0\bigr),\quad X_{vv} = \bigl(-u\cos v,\, -u\sin v,\, 0\bigr) \] \[ e = \frac{-1}{u\sqrt{1+u^2}},\quad f = 0,\quad g = \frac{u}{\sqrt{1+u^2}},\quad E = 1 + \frac{1}{u^2},\quad F = 0,\quad G = u^2 \] \[ K_1 = \frac{-1}{(1+u^2)^2} \] \[ Y_u = (\cos v, \sin v, 0),\quad Y_v = (-u\sin v, u\cos v, 1),\quad E = 1,\ F = 0,\ G = 1+u^2 \] \[ N = \frac{(\sin v, -\cos v, u)}{\sqrt{1+u^2}} \] \[ Y_{uu} = (0,0,0),\quad Y_{uv} = (-\sin v, \cos v, 0),\quad e = 0,\ f = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+u^2}} \] \[ K_2 = -\frac{1}{(1+u^2)^2} \]

The first fundamental form is essentially a way to measure the norm of the tangent vector to a curve.

\[ \begin{aligned} |\gamma'|^2 &= E\left(\frac{du}{dt}\right)^2 + 2F \frac{du}{dt}\frac{dv}{dt} + G\left(\frac{dv}{dt}\right)^2 \\ &= E\bigl(u_x x' + u_y y'\bigr)^2 + 2F\bigl(u_x x' + u_y y'\bigr)\bigl(v_x x' + v_y y'\bigr) \\ &\quad + G\bigl(v_x x' + v_y y'\bigr)^2 \\ &= \tilde{E} x'^2 + 2\tilde{F} x'y' + \tilde{G} y'^2 \\ &= \bigl(E u_x^2 + 2F u_x v_x + G v_x^2\bigr) x'^2 + 2\bigl(E u_x u_y + F(u_x v_y + u_y v_x) \\ &\quad + G v_x v_y\bigr) x'y' + \bigl(E u_y^2 + 2F u_y v_y + G v_y^2\bigr) y'^2 \end{aligned} \] \[ \begin{pmatrix} \tilde{E} & \tilde{F} \\ \tilde{F} & \tilde{G} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} u_x & u_y \\ v_x & v_y \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} E & F \\ F & G \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_x & v_x \\ u_y & v_y \end{pmatrix} \] \[ \mathrm{I} = E\,du^2 + 2F\,du\,dv + G\,dv^2, \quad du = u_x dx + u_y dy,\quad dv = v_x dx + v_y dy \]

Narrative

Poincaré disc:

\[ D = \{(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid u^2 + v^2 < 1\} \] \[ \mathrm{I}^D = \frac{4}{\bigl(1 - (u^2 + v^2)\bigr)^2}\,(du^2 + dv^2) \left[ = \frac{4}{\bigl(1 - |z|^2\bigr)^2}\,dz\,d\bar{z} \quad,\quad u+iv = z \right] \]

\[ U = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid y > 0\} \] \[ \mathrm{I}^U = \frac{dx^2 + dy^2}{y^2} = \left[ \frac{dw\,d\bar{w}}{\bigl(Im\ w\bigr)^2} \quad,\quad w = x+iy \right] \]

\[ \varphi: D \to \mathcal{U},\quad z \mapsto w = i \frac{1-z}{1+z} \quad \left[ z = \frac{i-w}{i+w} \right] \] \[ dz = -\frac{2i\,dw}{(i+w)^2},\quad d\bar{z} = \frac{2i\,d\bar{w}}{(-i+\bar{w})^2} \]

Now the key in our study of surfaces was to describe, out of the definition, the notion of the tangent space.

Narrative

You cannot speak about the derivative of a function with values on a set because you cannot even take the difference. So we have to give another interpretation of tangent vectors. Actually the idea is really to save the idea of velocity, but somehow we have to change the interpretation.

\[ \alpha: (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^n,\quad \alpha(0) = p. \] \[ \alpha(t) = \bigl(x_1(t), \dots, x_n(t)\bigr) \] \[ \alpha'(0) = \bigl(x_1', \dots, x_n'\bigr)(0) = v \]

If \(\varphi\) is a function around \(p\), the derivative of \(\varphi\) in the \(v\)-direction

\[ \left.\frac{d\varphi \circ \alpha}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = \sum_{i=1}^n \left.\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_i} \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial t}\right|_{t=0} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i'(0) \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right)(\varphi) \]

Then the point is to prove, logically, this object does not depend on \(\alpha\), but only on \(v\).

Narrative

This kind of differential operator is completely determined by \(v\) because its coefficients with respect to the partial derivatives are given exactly by the components of the vector \(v\). So knowing \(v\) and knowing this operator is the same thing. If I give the interpretation that the tangent vector is not something I draw as I'm used to but as an operator, a differential operator on functions which satisfies certain properties, then I have a hope.

Definition

Example

\(\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}) = M\)

\[ U_1 = \bigl\{ (x_1, x_2, x_3) \mid x_1 > 0,\ x_2^2 + x_3^2 < 1 \bigr\} \] \[ f_1^+(x_2, x_3) = \bigl(\sqrt{1 - x_2^2 - x_3^2},\ x_2,\ x_3\bigr) \] \[ f_1^-(x_2, x_3) = \bigl(-\sqrt{1 - x_2^2 - x_3^2},\ x_2,\ x_3\bigr) \] \[ \pi: S^2 \to \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R})\quad p \mapsto [p],\quad \pi(f_i^+(u_i)) = \pi(f_i^-(u_i)) \]

So we can define \(g_i: U_i \to \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}),\ g_i = \pi \circ f_i^+\)

\[ \bigl(\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}), \{(U_\alpha, f_\alpha)\}\bigr), \bigl(\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}), \{(U_i, g_i)\}\bigr)\text{ are diffeomorphic.} \]

This is one moment where you have to think about the famous third property in the definition of differentiable structure. These atlases are very different so they have the same differentiable structure. If the differentiable structure is just the collection of these sets, then they are different. But the maximal cover with all those properties will be the same.

\[ \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}) \not\hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 \] \[ \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^4 \]

Not every two-dimensional manifold is a submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

Is it true that any differentiable manifold can be embedded into some Euclidean space, letting the dimension free? The answer is yes.

This was historically a key question. Because really you are comparing is the new geometry with the old geometry in some sense.

Chapter: Global Differential Geometry

\(\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R})\)

Narrative

We defined one differentiable structure even though we presented it in two different ways on \(\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R})\). One was coming naturally looking at it as \(\mathbb{R}^3\) minus the origin quotient by the equivalence relation and the other was thinking of it as the quotient of \(S^2\) modulo the antipodal map. This induces naturally two seemingly different differentiable structures, but it's easy to check that they are actually diffeomorphic.

Whitney theorem: every compact differentiable manifold is in fact a submanifold of a sufficiently big dimensional \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

In fact, in general, if you take a compact n-dimensional manifold \(M^n\), this will always embed inside \(\mathbb{R}^{2n+1}\).

\[ M^n \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2n+1} \] \[ \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^4 \] \[ \varphi: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^4,\quad (x,y,z) \mapsto (x^2-y^2,\, xy,\, xz,\, yz) \quad \text{on } S^2. \]

\(\varphi\) passed to the quotient giving \(\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R})\).

This map \(\varphi\) passed to the quotient when I restricted to \(S^2\).

\[ \theta: \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^4. \]

This will be formally the quotient map of \(\varphi\). So now the claim is that this is actually an embedding.

\[ f_3^+(x,y) \mapsto \bigl(x,y,\ \overset{D}{\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}}\bigr) \quad \text{in the disk}, \] \[ \varphi \circ f_3^+ = \bigl(x^2-y^2,\ xy,\ xD,\ yD\bigr) \]

I need to prove that differential is injective.

\(d(\varphi \circ f_3^+)\) is represented by \(\begin{pmatrix} 2x & y & D+xD_x & yD_x \\ -2y & x & xD_y & D + y D_y \end{pmatrix}\)

Now the question is, has this matrix rank 2 at every point? Yes.

So it's a differentiable map, it's an immersion, it's one-to-one, it's continuous. You would need to prove that it's a homeomorphism onto its image.

Narrative

Is it possible for two differentiable structures to induce the same topology but they are not diffeomorphic? Meaning, the association from differentiable structure to topological structure, is it injective in some sense? So the basic of the question is, is it possible that two homeomorphic manifolds are not diffeomorphic? For surfaces, you can prove that this is not possible. And the answer is actually yes, even for compact manifold, and in fact, even for very simple topological manifolds.

Milnor: If you take \(S^n\), \(n \ge 7\), these topological spaces have differentiable structures which are not diffeomorphic. These are called exotic structures (Milnor, 1954).

Donaldson — (Freedman), 1984

Exotic structures exist on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) only for \(n=4\).
